title: Harnessing gasotransmitters for orthopaedic infection therapy: Mechanisms and advanced delivery platforms
abstract: Orthopaedic infections are increasingly prevalent in the aging population, posing a significant clinical and economic burden. Despite progress in antimicrobial therapies, challenges such as antibiotic resistance and superbug emergence persist. Gas therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for managing orthopaedic infections. Classical gasotransmitters-including nitric oxide (NO), carbon monoxide (CO), and hydrogen sulfide (HS)-exhibit antibacterial and immunomodulatory effects at controlled concentrations, though improper dosing may induce adverse effects. This review critically examines the dual mechanisms through which gasotransmitters combat infection while promoting orthopaedic regeneration. We also survey advanced delivery platforms-such as smart scaffolds, nano-reservoirs, and on-demand release systems-engineered for targeted gasotransmitter delivery to infected bone tissue. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future prospects, aiming to inspire novel biomaterial designs for targeted therapeutic delivery and to advance gas therapy as a viable option for orthopaedic infection treatment.

title: Bioprinted core-shell living material platform for spatially controlled encapsulation of Bacillus subtilis and sustained metabolite exchange
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating global health crisis, demanding alternative strategies to reduce resistant pathogen burden across environments. Microbe-based biocontrol is promising, yet effectively deploying it in practical settings remains challenging. In this study, we present a 3D bioprinted core-shell construct featuring a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) shell with tunable nanoscale porosity, encapsulating germinable spores of the biocontrol agentTH035. This configuration supports long-term spore viability while providing protection from common environmental stressors including UV-C irradiation, ethanol exposure, and desiccation over 4 weeks. The nanoporous PEGDA shell enables effective bacterial confinement while facilitating sufficient metabolite exchange forgermination and growth, as well as suppression of methicillin-resistant(MRSA) growth by approximately one order of magnitude. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of embeddingspores within engineered scaffolds for extended competitive functionality. The versatility and scalability of digital light processing (DLP) based bioprinting offers significant potential for tailored designs and high-throughput manufacturing. This proof-of-concept platform may find future applications in areas such as biomedical packaging, environmental sanitation, and built environment surface coatings, particularly in settings where intermittent moisture or nutrient availability can support spore germination and biocontrol activity.

title: Artificial intelligence catalyzes antimicrobial peptide design
abstract: With broad-spectrum, low resistance, and multifunctional properties, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising therapeutic agents against drug-resistant pathogens, yet their discovery and optimization still remain challenging due to the complexity of sequence-function associations. Artificial intelligence (AI), through the construction of comprehensive data-driven models that assisted with miscellaneous learning strategies, enables de novo peptide design by learning latent representations inherent in peptide sequences as well as their biological properties to ensure physically plausible and biologically relevant predictions. Consequently, this paradigm enhances the likelihood of designing peptide candidates with significantly improved therapeutic potential, reducing resource-intensive trial-and-error processes and revealing the transformative impact of computational innovation in advancing next-generation therapeutics. Here, we provide a snapshot of this field and survey two modes of AI-driven technologies for AMP design, one concentrated on identifying whether current data possess antimicrobial activity (identification-oriented) and the other on generating AMP candidates with potential therapeutic properties (generation-oriented). We also highlight the challenges and limitations that still hinder AMP development even accelerated by AI, as well as the foreseeable prospects, from finer-grained explorations to model-driven data enrichment and model enhancement.

title: Antifungal mechanisms of volatile organic compounds and lactic acid produced by Lactiplantibacillus pentosus and their biocontrol application in fresh corn against Fusarium graminearum
abstract: Fusarium graminearum causes cereal spoilage and mycotoxin production. Currently, biocontrol microorganisms have emerged as a safe and promising strategy to manage the contamination of toxin-producing fungi in cereal grains. The primary objective was to elucidate the antifungal mechanism of an isolated strain of Lactiplantibacillus pentosus Q11 against F. graminearum and to evaluate the preservative effects of its cell-free supernatant (CFS) in fresh sweet corn. In vitro antifungal assays of L. pentosus Q11 showed strong antagonistic activity against F. graminearum, Aspergillus flavus, and Penicillium expansum, as well as the ability to reduce zearalenone. Moreover, whole-genome analysis revealed no genes related to virulence and antimicrobial resistance, and no hemolytic activity was observed, which suggested the potential safety of strain Q11. Moreover, the CFS of L. pentosus Q11 effectively inhibited the mycelial growth of F. graminearum, disrupted hyphal integrity, and induced fungal cell death. Moreover, 3 organic acids and 38 volatile compounds in the CFS of Q11 strain were identified by SPME-GC-MS and HPLC, in which 2-nonanone, 2-methylpyrazine, lactic acid, acetic acid were predominant compounds. The CFS and lactic acid combined with 2-nonanone severely damaged hyphae of F. graminearum, by disrupting cell membrane and wall, leading to leakage of intracellular substances, showing a synergistic antifungal effect of the two vital compounds. Subsequently, the treatments of CFS and combined agents significantly decreased 88.05% - 89.52% of fungal populations, and AFBand DON mycotoxin accumulation in fresh sweet corn after 12 days of storage compared to the control. The malondialdehyde content in the treated corn was decreased by 29.25% - 31.50%, consistent with the higher activities of POD and APX, thereby preserving their sensory attributes and nutritional quality. Metabolomic analysis revealed that L-glutamate, γ-glutamylcysteine, and oxidized glutathione were significantly downregulated in the glutathione metabolism pathway in the treated corn, indicating that CFS containing lactic acid and 2-nonanone could repress fungal growth and alleviate oxidative stress in fresh sweet corn. Overall, these findings demonstrate that L. pentosus Q11 with synergistic volatile organic compounds and lactic acid is a promising biocontrol agent in preserving fresh sweet corn.

Strengthening antimicrobial stewardship through an international multicentre improvement programme of hospitals serving deprived populations
abstract: Antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) is essential to addressing antimicrobial resistance, but its implementation remains variable, particularly in settings with resource limitations. Hospitals serving deprived or underserved populations often work with limited diagnostic capacity, workforce pressures and variable digital infrastructure, which shape stewardship delivery. The Antimicrobial Stewardship Disparities Programme (ASDP) was established to strengthen stewardship capability in such settings and to support progress towards accreditation under the Global AMS Accreditation Scheme (GAMSAS). A mixed-methods evaluation was undertaken across six centres in Botswana, Kenya, Lebanon, Mexico, Pakistan and the USA. Centres completed baseline and end of programme self-assessments against 17 AMS, infection prevention and control (IPC) and laboratory standards mapped to 4 pillars (structures, guidance, education and surveillance). Programme documentation was analysed to identify themes, contextual influences and barriers. All work was delivered within existing resources. Centres achieved improvements across AMS, IPC and laboratory standards, with consistent progress in surveillance. Governance was strengthened through clearer AMS committee structures, and guidance improved through prescribing tools embedded in practice. Education and laboratory standards showed limited change, reflecting workforce pressures, lack of protected time and constrained diagnostic capacity. Three centres achieved GAMSAS accreditation. Qualitative findings highlighted strategies to advance stewardship within structural constraints, including surveillance systems, training and locally adapted guidance. Local aims, supported by a standards framework and mentorship, enabled centres to strengthen stewardship capability within existing resources. Workforce capacity, diagnostic access and digital infrastructure remain key determinants. Structured assessment and shared learning support scalable AMS in underserved settings.

abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is escalating in East Africa through close human-animal-environment interactions. Extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBL) and carbapenemase-producingare clinically critical pathogens, yet local evidence is limited. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on ESBL and carbapenemase-producingin East Africa to inform One Health AMR control strategies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, PubMed and Scopus were searched, identifying 279 records published between 2015 and 2025. After removing duplicates and screening, 185 articles were assessed for eligibility; 154 studies spanning human, animal and environmental sources met the inclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently extracted epidemiological, microbiological and molecular data in Covidence, including resistance genes and transmission evidence. The 154 included studies spanned 11 East African countries, led by Ethiopia ( = 55), Tanzania ( = 39) and Uganda ( = 22). Most studies (85.7%) were cross-sectional and human-focused (68.2%), with only 19 (12.3%) using a multi-sector One Health design. Overall, 21,554isolates were recovered from 74,700 samples. ESBL prevalence was reported in 117 studies (76.0%, median 46.8%) and carbapenemase prevalence in 65 (42.2%, median 3.3%), representing heterogeneous study-level estimates.predominated (89.9%), led by(26.1%); reported carbapenemase genes included,,andWhole-genome sequencing in 30 studies (19.5%) identified high-risk clones ST131, ST10, ST38 and ST410, though animal, food-chain and environmental sectors remained underrepresented. This review maps the current evidence on landscape for ESBL/carbapenemase- producingin East Africa, highlighting gaps in surveillance that are largely due to heterogeneity of available genomics data and limited longitudinal data within the "One Health" sectors. We recommend scaling up genomic capacity and standardized longitudinal surveillance to better understand national and regional AMR transmission and MDRinfections.

title: Dietary licorice improves carcass yield, hepatocellular protection, gut health, oxidative status, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens
abstract: Over the past decade, phytotherapy such as licorice has attracted research as an alternative to antibiotic growth promoters in broiler production, driven by rising concerns over antimicrobial resistance. However, the consistency of its effects across productive, physiological, and health outcomes remains inconsistent. This meta-analysis quantitatively synthesized published experimental evidence on the effects of dietary licorice on growth performance, carcass yield, blood indices, visceral organs, oxidative status, intestinal morphology, and cecal bacterial balance in broiler chickens. A systematic literature search identified studies published between 2010 and 2025, and effect sizes were computed (Hedges'; 95% confidence interval). Pooled estimates were derived under the random-effects model using the restricted maximum likelihood estimator, with between-study heterogeneity characterized bythe-statistic. Univariable mixed-effects meta-regression was conducted to identify study-level moderators of treatment response, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot and the Rosenberg fail-safe N criterion. Dietary licorice did not affect feed intake or the feed conversion ratio, but it did increase body weight gain (BWG; SMD = 0.289; = 0.002), breast, thigh, gizzard, and bursa weights ( < 0.05). Gut integrity also improved with the villus height/crypt depth ratio (SMD = 0.931; = 0.041), andspp. counts (SMD = 0.266; = 0.003) increased, whilepopulations were suppressed (SMD = -1.737; < 0.001). Overall, the findings support that licorice enhances body weight gain, with route, duration, sex, and strain moderating efficacy.

abstract: ()is a globally pervasive and economically significant pathogen in bovine intramammary infections (IMIs) and is responsible for both clinical and subclinical mastitis. This study systematically investigated the global epidemiology offrom bovine IMIs, addressing antimicrobial resistance (AMR) amongthrough a meta-analysis. A total of 143 studies published between 2000 and 2025 were identified through comprehensive searches, which were based on predefined inclusion criteria. The data were systematically extracted, and the statistical analyses were performed in R (v4.5.2). The meta-analysis included 143 studies (145,457 samples), with a pooledprevalence of 24.78% and high heterogeneity (I = 99.51%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant heterogeneity in prevalence by study design, publication year, and region, with greater heterogeneity in cross-sectional studies (I>95%, < 0.001). Meta-regression identified sample size as a significant source of heterogeneity (β = -0.00002, = 0.02; R = 3.41%). The highest prevalence was reported in Cameroon (67%), Sri Lanka (64.3%), Indonesia (57%), and India (44%), with the lowest prevalence reported in Poland (0.7%), Taiwan (2.0%), Australia (5.5%), and New Zealand (5.3%). AMR was highest for doxycycline (70.7%), penicillin (65.2%), and ampicillin (62.8%); moderate to oxacillin (44.6%) and vancomycin (40.2%); and lowest for gentamicin (27.5%) and amikacin (18.3%). is highly prevalent in bovine IMIs worldwide, with marked regional heterogeneity and substantial resistance to commonly used antimicrobials, emphasizing the urgent need for targeted surveillance, prudent antimicrobial use, and improved mastitis control strategies at the global and regional levels.

N-acetylcysteine as an adjunct to antibiotics against bacterial biofilms: A systematic review of in vitro evidence
abstract: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is investigated as an antibiotic adjunct, but acidity, formulation and experimental context complicate interpretation. We evaluated comparative in-vitro evidence while distinguishing biofilm prevention, established-biofilm treatment and resistance evolution. MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Web of Science were searched through August 2026, with supplementary searching. Extraction distinguished NAC preparation and exposure pH, medium, hydrodynamics, NAC-alone controls, treatment intent and interaction methodology. Results were synthesized by experimental context, regimen, phase and endpoint without pooling or whole-study efficacy voting. Fifty-five studies were included: 7 evaluated combination exposure during formation only, 37 after establishment only, 9 both, and 2 resistance evolution. NAC-alone arms were documented in 39 studies, partial or formulation-specific in 9, and not identified in 7. Only two studies included a continuous-flow model. Selected combinations improved biofilm-associated outcomes, but intrinsic-acidic and neutralized preparations, biomass and viability endpoints, and planktonic versus biofilm interaction tests were not interchangeable. Liposomal and catheter-lock findings differed by dose matching, isolate and control set. Polymyxin findings varied with organism, resistance background, medium and exposure; rifampicin-alone and rifampicin-containing multidrug comparators addressed different questions. NAC is a context-dependent experimental adjunct, not an established class-wide antibiotic potentiator. The evidence does not support clinical antibiotic dose reduction or routine NAC combination therapy. Translation requires controlled final exposure pH, matched monotherapy and formulation controls, clinically relevant background regimens, viable-burden and regrowth outcomes, and resistance monitoring.

Combating antimicrobial resistance through multimodal data via artificial intelligence
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses a critical global health challenge, leading to substantial mortality and economic losses without science-based interventions. Conventional approaches to combating AMR have important limitations in addressing this escalating threat. Recent advances in AI, including deep learning, large language models, and protein language models, provide new opportunities to integrate multimodal data for AMR research. However, evidence remains uneven, with many approaches limited to computational benchmarking rather than real-world validation. Here, we critically review AI applications in AMR, focusing on rapid diagnosis, therapeutic discovery, and clinical decision support. AI-based diagnostic models can identify resistant pathogens and predict resistance profiles, but most lack prospective clinical evaluation. AI-assisted drug discovery and alternative therapies have generated promising candidates, although most remain at computational, in vitro, or early preclinical stages. Large language models may support decision-making, but their clinical use remains preliminary. Successful translation of AI into clinical and One Health practice will require representative datasets, independent validation, prospective evaluation, and robust governance.

Strengthening One Health Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance in Bangladesh: Insights from the Fleming fund country grant
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an escalating global public health concern, with particularly severe implications for low and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh. In Bangladesh context, fragmented surveillance systems and the extensive use of antimicrobials across human, animal, and aquaculture sectors contribute to the rapid emergence and spread of resistance. Strengthening integrated surveillance through a One Health approach is therefore crucial to support effective policy development and response strategies. This review outlines the policy, implementation, and key outcomes of the Fleming Fund Country Grant in Bangladesh between 2020 and 2025. It draws upon multiple data sources, including programme reports, routine AMR surveillance data, laboratory capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder engagement activities across human, animal, aquaculture, and environmental sectors. Through this initiative, a coordinated national AMR surveillance network was established, comprising 20 laboratories across multiple sectors, including three designated national reference laboratories. The initiative strengthened surveillance through the introduction of standardized protocols and SOPs, improved diagnostic capacity, skilled workforce, and implementation of laboratory quality assurance systems, including EQA and NEQA. These measures enhanced the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of AMR surveillance data. In addition, the establishment of a national AMR data integration platform facilitated real time data sharing and evidence-based decision-making. A total of 208,346 bacterial isolates were analyzed, with AST results reported to the AMR dashboard across the human, and animal, health sectors. Overall, the Fleming Fund programme has made a substantial contribution to strengthening integrated AMR surveillance in Bangladesh by operationalizing a One Health framework. Continued political commitment, increased domestic investment, and the institutionalization of surveillance systems will be essential to sustain these gains and ensure long-term resilience against AMR.

Microfluidic-assembled curcumin ionizable lipid nanoparticles enhance aqueous delivery and antibiofilm activity against Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections demand novel therapeutic strategies. Curcumin is a natural polyphenol with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity; however, its clinical utility is fundamentally constrained by negligible aqueous solubility and limited biofilm penetration. Here, we used microfluidic assembly to prepare curcumin-loaded ionizable lipid nanoparticles (Cur@LNP) with three clinically established ionizable lipids (SM-102, MC-3, and ALC-0315). The resulting formulations were uniform, with hydrodynamic diameters of approximately 90 nm and polydispersity indices near 0.1. Relative to free curcumin in DMSO, Cur@LNP lowered the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) 8-fold and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) 16-fold against planktonic, and markedly reduced viable biofilm-resident cells at matched concentrations. Scanning electron microscopy showed that Cur@LNP treatment remodeled mature biofilms into irregular, debris-rich aggregates with reduced extracellular matrix coverage. Notably, antimicrobial performance was indistinguishable across the three structurally distinct ionizable lipids at every concentration tested. Within this in vitro, single-strain system, the antibiofilm effect is therefore dominated by the cargo (curcumin) rather than by ionizable-lipid chemistry, and it is most likely attributed to enhanced aqueous solubilization of curcumin rather than to engagement of the lipid headgroup with the biofilm matrix. These results position microfluidic-assembled ionizable LNPs as a reproducible, scalable solubilization platform for poorly water-soluble natural antimicrobials.

title: Metagenomic analysis of commensal small mammal samples from an international cargo shipping area, Bangkok Port, reveals potential zoonotic pathogens and implications for One Health surveillance
abstract: Commensal small mammals, such as rats and shrews, are recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens; however, their role in pathogen circulation at transport hubs remains underexplored. This study employs shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize microbial communities and assess zoonotic potential in tissue samples from commensal small mammals captured at Bangkok Port, an international cargo shipping hub in Thailand between June and August 2025. Following host read depletion, taxonomic profiling was performed to identify bacterial taxa of public health relevance, including sequences assigned tospp.,,, and. The virulence factor and antibiotic resistance gene profiles revealed that some of these pathogens have pathogenic potential and are related to drug-resistant bacteria. In addition,was identified as a shared taxon among rats, shrews, and their associated fleas. The findings support the ecological roles of mammalian hosts and their ectoparasites as reservoirs for pathogens of public health concern. These results emphasize the need to strengthen surveillance programs for commensal small mammals to monitor and mitigate the spread of transboundary pathogens at international maritime gateways.

Wild boar as a sentinel species for ecosystem health surveillance: A review
abstract: Sentinel surveillance uses selected species that are widely distributed, easily sampled, and exposed to multiple health threats as indicators of ecosystem health. The Eurasian wild boar () is a broadly distributed game species that meets these conditions. We conducted a systematic review to assess the suitability of the wild boar as a sentinel or indicator species for monitoring health hazards relevant to ecosystem health, focusing on the hazards monitored, methods, justification for use, perceived performance, limitations, and proposed improvements. We identified 86 studies explicitly framing the wild boar as a sentinel species, covering a wide range of hazards, including 30 pathogens, 44 environmental contaminants, two biological toxins and 13 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) indicators. It was used to monitor pathogens (57%), environmental contaminants (31.4%), AMR (12.8%), and biological toxins (3.5%). Research effort was concentrated in Europe (84.9%) and relied mostly on hunted animals (90.7%). Wild boar were frequently selected as sentinels due to their previous use as indicators of ecosystem health in the literature, omnivorous diet, wide distribution, and accessibility as game species. However, hunting-based sampling may introduce biases, while post-mortem conditions and ecological variability may affect results. Despite this, 74.4% of studies supported their use as sentinels, particularly for pathogens and environmental contaminants. In contrast, their perceived suitability for AMR was more variable, and no quality assessment was available for biological toxins. Overall, wild boar sentinel surveillance is considered logistically efficient and valuable for monitoring ecosystem health hazards. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent and influenced by methodological and ecological limitations. Improving surveillance design through systematic sampling, alternative sample sources (e.g., found-dead animals or non-invasive methods), integration of multi-species data, and inclusion of covariates could enhance the reliability of findings within a One Health framework.

title: Global spread of carbapenem-resistant Providencia driven by high-risk lineages and plasmid co-evolution
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant(CRP) is a formidable opportunistic pathogen with extensive drug resistance, posing an increasing threat to human, animal, and environmental health. However, its global genomic epidemiology and resistome-plasmidome co-evolution within a One Health context remain poorly understood. Here, we conducted a comprehensive population genomic and plasmid analysis of 1197 CRP isolates from 35 countries spanning 2012-2025. We reclassified the CRP population into ninespecies, identifyingandas established epidemic species alongside the rapid emergence ofand. We pinpointed 2019 as a critical inflection point, marking the transition from endemic stability to rapid global epidemic expansion (80.8% isolates in 2019-2025). Ten intercontinentally disseminated high-risk sequence types (e.g., ST46, ST79), each with strict species-ST specificity, were responsible for global spread. Thegene (62.4% prevalence) was the predominant carbapenem gene, exhibiting strong geographic and species specificity and mutual exclusion with other major carbapenem genes. Plasmids encoded approximately 80% of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, with 78.0% of these plasmids belonging to 75 stable clusters. These clusters evolved a dual specialist-generalist strategy, with the broad-host-range cluster 72 mediating interspecies AMR transmission and cluster 7 acting as a super-vector carrying six carbapenem genes. Importantly, CRP circulated across interconnected human, animal, and environmental reservoirs, with distinct host-associated species distributions suggesting ecological niche adaptation and potential cross-host dissemination of resistance determinants. These findings demonstrate that the global expansion of CRP is driven by the combined evolution of high-risk clones and mobile genetic elements across interconnected ecological sectors, underscoring the need for integrated One Health surveillance and coordinated interventions spanning clinical, veterinary, agricultural, and environmental settings.

title: Management of pneumonia by the emergency radiologist
Exploring veterinarian and pet owner perspectives on the risk of antimicrobial resistance when feeding raw meat diets to dogs
Prevalence and genomic characterization of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium across a duck breeder-hatchery-grow-out production system in China
Five years of wastewater surveillance reveal COVID-19-Associated amplification and seasonal shifts in bla (KPC) and bla (NDM)
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has intensified in recent years, raising concerns about the potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on AMR dynamics. However, the influence of pandemic on the enviromental occurrence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant genes (ARGs) remains under investigation. Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) provides an integrated view of community-level AMR dynamics, yet long-term assessments spanning the pandemic period remain limited. This study investigated the occurrence, temporal patterns, and seasonal behavior of two clinically relevant carbapenemase genes,and, in raw wastewater from the Attica region over a five-year period (July 2021-September 2025). A sensitive and specific 3-plex qPCR assay was developed and analytically validated for the simultaneous quantification of,, and 16S rRNA, the latter serving as a stable bacterial load indicator. Across the monitoring period,was consistently detected, showing a steady increase and reaching its highest concentrations in 2023, whileexhibited intermittent but pronounced surges, particularly in 2023. Comparison with community SARS-CoV-2 viral loads suggest temporal association with AMR signatures in wastewater. Seasonal analysis showed non-uniform patterns, with atypical warm-season peaks of both ARGs in 2023-2024 and a return to classical autumn-winter peaks in 2025, suggesting a gradual restoration of pre-pandemic seasonality. To our knowledge, this is among the first long-term WBE studies to characterize post-COVID-19 shifts in ARG occurrence and seasonality. The results demonstrate that the pandemic period was associated with elevated and fluctuating ARG levels in the urban wastewater system, emphasizing the need for sustained AMR monitoring. These findings address critical knowledge gaps in environmental AMR surveillance and support the integration of WBE into public health strategies aimed at mitigating AMR dissemination.

title: Prevalence of antimicrobial-resistant Escherichia coli as an indicator bacterium in livestock and companion animals in Mongolia
Genomic epidemiology to investigate the origins and zoonotic implications of antibiotic-resistant Escherichia coli on beef and lamb meat sold by independent butchers in Wales
abstract: Many studies have identified antibiotic resistant (ABR)on meat. Appropriate hand hygiene and cooking practices should minimize the risk of gastrointestinal colonisation with ABRfound on meat, and the subsequent chance of causing resistant opportunistic extraintestinal infection. There are large gaps in our understanding of the prevalence, origins and zoonotic potential of ABRfound on meat, however, and particularly for meat reared in extensive farming systems. Wales is a devolved nation within the United Kingdom having large populations of extensively-reared sheep and beef cattle. To help address knowledge gaps around ABRon extensively reared meat, therefore, beef mince and lamb loin/leg steaks/chops were purchased from 50 (beef) and 46 (lamb) independent butchers across Wales. Following enrichment culture, 200 g meat samples were found to be positive forresistant to amoxicillin (31% positivity), streptomycin (28%), spectinomycin (29%), amoxicillin-clavulanate (11%), 3rd generation cephalosporins (2%) and fluoroquinolones (5%). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed that Welsh lamb meat ABRisolates ( = 78) are more closely related to those found in faecal samples collected around sheep ( = 352) than around beef cattle ( = 361) on Welsh farms. This suggests that faecal contamination at or around slaughter is their primary origin. We found no closely related meat/infection clones (<20 SNPs distant and the same antibiotic resistance genes) when comparing ABRfrom Welsh meat ( = 91) and those causing extraintestinal infections in people ( = 2387) in an English region bordering Wales. We conclude, therefore, that the wider zoonotic implications of finding ABRon beef and lamb meat sold at independent butchers in Wales are small, though a more geographically and temporarily contemporaneous survey is warranted to address this further.

title: Genomic insights into activated antimicrobial resistance of in situ hospital-wastewater biofilm
Risk ranking and antimicrobial resistance of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli of bovine origin
Remote realities: In-depth conversations on antimicrobial stewardship in remote Indigenous communities using a One Health approach
Sewage surveillance for assessing clinical antibiotic resistance prevalence: Combining metagenomic and phenotypic data
abstract: Surveillance of antibiotic resistance in clinical isolates is a cornerstone for the management of bacterial infections but is limited in large parts of the world, often due to lack of resources. Sewage surveillance has been proposed as a promising, resource-efficient complement to the traditional surveillance approach based on samples from many individual patients. Both phenotypic data on resistance in sewage isolates and abundance of antibiotic resistance genes in sewage have been shown to correlate with resistance prevalence in clinical isolates. Here, we aimed to directly compare and combine an isolate-based and a gene-based sewage surveillance approach to evaluate what best can reflect clinical resistance rates. The two approaches, based on susceptibility testing of collectedisolates and metagenomic sequencing, respectively, were applied to municipal sewage samples collected in ten European countries. The data generated was related to available data on resistance to aminopenicillins, fluoroquinolones, third generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides prevalence in clinicalisolates using beta regression models. None of the tested individual predictors were superior across all four investigated classes of antibiotics. For modelling of aminopenicillin resistance, a clearly higher Rvalue was obtained when isolate-based and gene-based data was combined as predictors, also after adjusting for the number of included variables. We conclude that there could be a value of including both isolate- and gene-based sewage data for predictions of resistance rates in clinical isolates, while emphasizing the value of linking predictors to specific species and classes of antibiotics.

title: Clonal diversity, virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes of Enterococcus faecalis and Klebsiella pneumoniae from urban rats in Malaysia
abstract: Peridomestic rats serve as important carriers of zoonotic pathogens, including multidrug-resistant bacteria such asand. However, information on the clonal diversity, antibiotic resistance, and virulence of these pathogens in wild urban rats remains limited, particularly in tropical settings. This study investigatedandin urban rats from wet markets across four Malaysian states. A total of 277 rats (, = 177;, = 100) were trapped, and lung tissues were processed for bacterial isolation. Isolates were identified by 16S rDNA sequencing and examined for antibiotic susceptibility, resistance genes, and virulence factors using PCR. Clonal relationships were determined through multilocus sequence typing (MLST). Nineteenand sevenisolates were recovered. Allisolates carried multiple virulence factors (,,, and), and four tetracycline-resistant isolates possessed,, and. Five novelsequence types (ST730 - ST734) were identified. Allisolates carried the SHV gene; two also harbored FOX, and two possessedandvirulence factors. Two novelSTs (ST2641 and ST2642) were detected. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that both species displayed diverse sequence types scattered across global lineages. These findings suggest that urban rats may act as potential carriers of virulent and antibiotic-resistantand. These findings support the inclusion of urban rats in future One Health surveillance programs investigating antimicrobial resistance and virulent bacterial pathogens.

title: Virulence attenuation in ST11-K64 Klebsiella pneumoniae explains its divergent clinical manifestation from ST23-K1
Design, synthesis, and antibacterial activity study of pyrroloquinazoline diamine derivatives
Antimicrobial resistance patterns and polymicrobial co-detection characteristics of vaginal Group B Streptococcus in pregnant women: a retrospective study
Genetic determinants of hypervirulence with attenuated pathogenicity in a bla(NDM-1)-encoding Klebsiella pneumoniae causing neonatal sepsis
Copper-coated carbon nanotube surfaces for inhibiting biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Biofilm-associated infections caused by clinically important pathogens such as() and() remain a major challenge in healthcare settings due to enhanced antimicrobial resistance and persistence. In recent years, copper-coated carbon nanotubes (Cu-CNTs) have gained considerable attention as promising antimicrobial nanomaterials for preventing biofilm formation on medical devices and hospital-associated surfaces. This review summarizes recent advances in the development and application of Cu-CNT-based antimicrobial coatings, with an emphasis on their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens. The synergistic combination of the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of CNTs and the potent antimicrobial properties of copper (Cu) ions enhances microbial inhibition. Previous studies suggest that Cu-CNTs interfere with initial bacterial adhesion, inhibit biofilm maturation, and disrupt established biofilms through mechanisms involving oxidative stress generation, membrane destabilization, and cellular damage. Furthermore, the review discusses the physicochemical characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, biomedical applications, and potential challenges associated with Cu-CNT coatings, including toxicity and biocompatibility concerns. Overall, Cu-CNT-based coatings represent a promising strategy for developing durable antimicrobial surfaces to control chronic biofilm-associated infections and reduce healthcare-associated contamination.

Synergistic antibacterial activity and mechanism of arginine combined with florfenicol against Escherichia coli
Differential modulation of gentamicin antibacterial activity by vitamin B12 and vitamin D3 against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria: an in vitro-in silico study
Artificial plastic substrate for tracking and exploring antimicrobial-resistant bacteria transmission pathways in aquatic ecosystems
abstract: Investigating the persistence and dissemination of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARBs) in aquatic ecosystems is challenging because conventional methods require large volumes of water, particularly difficult to collect in regions affected by climate-related stress. This study developed and evaluated artificial plastic substrates (APSs) as an effective sampling tool and assessed the potential role of plastic as a transmission vector for ARBs. Five monthly sampling campaigns were conducted at three sites along the Arrone River. A total of 127 ARBs, including extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacteriaceae andspp., were isolated from APSs and raw water (RW) and characterized at the microbiological and molecular levels. APSs recovered more ARBs than RW and captured key antibiotic resistance genes, including class 1 integrons and genes associated with β-lactam, carbapenem, tetracycline, sulfonamide, aminoglycoside, chloramphenicol, and efflux pump-mediated resistance. Overall, APSs proved to be an efficient, cost-effective, reproducible, and minimally invasive tool for monitoring ARBs and ARGs in aquatic ecosystems.

title: High-risk ARGs in environmental E. coli from the Taihu Lake watershed
Antibiotic resistance genes in aquaculture: Molecular detection, environmental dynamics, and biological control strategies
Bridging soil resistome and clinical inference: A four-tier evidentiary framework
Harnessing hydrogel technology for advanced periodontitis therapy: A multifunctional approach to oral health restoration
abstract: Periodontitis is a bacterially driven inflammatory disease that can lead to tooth mobility and tooth loss. Conventional non-surgical therapy, antibiotics, and surgery may be limited by residual subgingival biofilms, antimicrobial resistance, and variable clinical outcomes. This review synthesizes recent studies of hydrogel-based systems for local periodontal therapy, focusing on stimuli-responsive release mechanisms, cargo-loading approaches, and regenerative outcomes in relevant animal models. Across these studies, hydrogels function as localized delivery matrices that can prolong retention at periodontal defects, regulate therapeutic exposure, and support tissue repair. We further evaluate translational considerations, including degradation behavior, long-termstability, and immunocompatibility. These findings position hydrogels as adaptable platforms for more precise periodontitis management and identify priorities for preclinical optimization before clinical translation.

title: Microbiota-constrained bacterial density limits phage infection in the gut and allows persistence of susceptible cells
abstract: With the rise of antibiotic resistance, bacteriophage-based treatments against bacterial infections have regained momentum. However, phage therapy has so far shown only moderate success in complex environments like the mammalian gut, where phages are particularly promising tools for microbiome engineering and specific elimination of opportunistic pathogens. Here, we use different murine models of intestinal colonization to quantitatively assess the minimal population size of susceptiblecells that is required for phage replication in the gut (replication threshold). We found that the composition of the intestinal microbiota is a key factor shaping phage-bacteria interactions by restricting the carrying capacity of susceptible host cells. We further demonstrate that the replication threshold enables coexistence of susceptible and resistant bacteria in phage-treated mice, with implications for phage-based applications in complex environments like the gut.

title: "Nano-in-Gel Platforms for the Topical Treatment of Staphylococcus aureus Skin Infections"
abstract: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is the leading cause of skin infections worldwide. Rising antimicrobial resistance limits the effectiveness of current treatments, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. In this context, Rifabutin (RFB), could be repurposed for skin infections based on its strong anti-staphylococcal activity. However, its low oral bioavailability, and the rapid capacity of bacteria to develop drug tolerance, makes necessary to find novel platforms to ensure antimicrobial efficacy. This work proposes the development of Nano-in-Gel drug delivery systems, integrating RFB-loaded nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) into gelatin hydrogels for topical administration. These composite materials combine the controlled release capacity of hydrogels with NLCs´ ability to maximize RFB clinical potential. RFB-loaded NLCs were prepared and characterized in terms of physicochemical properties and cytocompatibility in human dermal fibroblasts (HDF). Moreover, their antibacterial activity against two different S. aureus strains-including mutants generated after RFB exposure was evaluated using a combination of conventional quantification methods and droplet digital PCR (ddPCR). Following the incorporation of NLCs into the gels, the mechanical properties of the Nano-in-Gel systems, and their ability to modulate nanoparticle release were assessed. Results demonstrated that the RFB-loaded NLCs possessed optimal physicochemical characteristics and high biocompatibility. Furthermore, the nanocarriers exhibited enhanced anti-staphylococcal activity compared to the free drug and successfully overcame RFB-resistance in mutant strains. The Nano-in-Gel platforms showed excellent mechanical performance for topical application and achieved a controlled NLCs release profile. These findings suggest that the Nano-in-Gel systems constitute a promising strategy for the advanced management of S. aureus skin infections.

title: HGSAF: Heterogeneous graph structural alignment and distillation model with attentive fusion for microbe-drug association prediction
abstract: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance necessitates AI-driven computational strategies to navigate the molecular diversity landscape of microbe-drug interactions. While graph neural networks have shown promise in predicting such associations, existing methods struggle with the intertwined challenges of processing topological and semantic features in isolation and handling severe class imbalance inherent in biomedical datasets. In this work, we devised a heterogeneous graph structural alignment and distillation with an attentive fusion model to predict microbe-drug associations. Our model constructs heterogeneous biological graphs alongside meta-path-induced subgraphs to capture complementary views of microbial and drug entities. A layer-adaptive graph transformer is devised to simultaneously encode topological and positional information while mitigating noise and over-smoothing. Critically, we introduce a reciprocal distillation module for dual-path heterogeneous graph learning that mutually transfers structural and semantic knowledge between pathways, eliminating the need for explicit negative sampling during representation alignment. For the final association prediction, unobserved pairs are sampled as negative examples for supervised training, following standard practice. A cross‑graph alignment loss, jointly optimized with focal loss, improves robustness against class imbalance under controlled sampling ratios (1:1 and 1:5). Extensive evaluations, including comparisons against both domain-specialized predictors and general-purpose graph neural network backbones, demonstrate that HGSAF consistently achieves superior performance and highlight the methodological robustness and potential for broader application in biomedical network analysis.

title: Vancomycin presoaking of ligament grafts: State of the Art and graft-specific evidence
abstract: Septic arthritis after ligament reconstruction is uncommon but potentially devastating. Vancomycin graft presoaking was developed as an adjunct to standard systemic prophylaxis and sterile technique to reduce viable Gram-positive contamination before implantation and biofilm maturation. This State-of-the-Art review evaluates its biological rationale, clinical effectiveness, safety, implementation, graft-specific considerations, hypersensitivity, antimicrobial stewardship, geographic variation, cost-effectiveness, and unresolved controversies. A structured narrative search of PubMed was updated through October 11, 2026, supplemented by backward citation screening and targeted review of relevant guidance and evidence syntheses. The clinical evidence remains predominantly observational. Large comparative cohorts and pooled analyses consistently associate vancomycin graft presoaking with lower rates of septic arthritis after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), with the most direct evidence applying to hamstring autografts. Limited randomized evidence is available but remains underpowered for a rare postoperative infection outcome. Absolute benefit varies with baseline infection risk. Laboratory, animal, and clinical studies have not demonstrated harm within commonly studied short-exposure protocols, although the most direct clinical safety evidence also derives from hamstring autografts. Evidence for bone-patellar tendon-bone grafts, quadriceps tendon grafts, allografts, revision procedures, and non-ACL ligament reconstructions remains substantially more limited or indirect. One uncontrolled 2026 quadriceps tendon series represents an unconfirmed graft-specific safety signal rather than evidence of a contraindication. No alternative graft-presoaking antibiotic currently has a clinical evidence base comparable to vancomycin. Based on the current evidence, vancomycin graft presoaking may be considered as an adjunct to standard systemic prophylaxis in hamstring autograft ACLR within a standardized protocol. It should not replace established infection-prevention measures, and extrapolation to other graft types or reconstruction settings should reflect the directness of the available evidence. Future research should prioritize graft-specific protocol optimization, prospective comparative evidence, antimicrobial-resistance surveillance, and long-term graft and cartilage outcomes.

title: Microbial and antimicrobial resistance signatures differentiate healthy and inflamed ileal pouches in patients with ulcerative colitis
abstract: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from healthy donors with a normally functioning colon has limited clinical effect in the treatment of chronic pouchitis. However, a normally functioning ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) physiology differs from individuals with a healthy intact colon. We aimed to investigate the microbial characteristics of patients with a normally functioning IPAA (HealthyPouch) compared with chronic pouchitis (SickPouch), ulcerative colitis (UC), and a healthy intact colon microbiome (NormalGut). Furthermore, we investigated how repeated antibiotic use influences antimicrobial resistance on a bacterial genome level. Fecal samples from 190 participants were collected; HealthyPouch (n = 38), SickPouch (n = 37), UC (n = 23), and NormalGut (n = 92) and sequenced with Illumina and taxonomically profiled. Samples from HealthyPouch, SickPouch, and NormalGut were also long-read sequenced using Oxford Nanopore Technologies for reconstruction of 12 282 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs). DNA methylation motifs were used for plasmid-host association. The HealthyPouch microbiome is distinct from both the UC, NormalGut, and SickPouch microbiome. Escherichia coli MAGs in the SickPouch (n = 21) microbiome had significantly higher co-occurring ciprofloxacin resistance mutations in the gyrA and parC genes, compared to both HealthyPouch (n = 26; BH adjusted P < .05) and NormalGut (n = 40; BH adjusted P < .05). Based on DNA methylation pattern, three plasmids were associated with E. coli carrying extended-spectrum beta lactamase genes. HealthyPouch microbiota differs from NormalGut microbiota, and could therefore be more appropriate for FMT treatment of chronic pouchitis. The association between E. coli and resistance gene-carrying plasmids underscores the importance of integrating plasmid analysis into metagenome-based approaches for personalized antibiotic treatment and resistance monitoring.

title: Quorum Sensing and Biofilm Regulation in ESKAPE Pathogens: Mechanisms, Therapeutic Targets, and Translational Challenges
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an emerging global health threat responsible for antibiotics being ineffective, leading to persistent infections, increased mortality, and healthcare costs. ESKAPE (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species) pathogens have a higher priority worldwide for the development of therapeutic approaches other than traditional antibiotics. Quorum sensing (QS) links population-dependent gene expression with a mechanistic understanding of bacterial communication, virulence regulation, and biofilm-associated persistence. Major QS systems across ESKAPE pathogens are Agr and accessory gene regulator networks in Gram-positive bacteria; LuxS/AI-2 signaling; the LuxI/LuxR-family systems in Gram-negative bacteria; the Las, Rhl, and Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) networks in P. aeruginosa; and the AbaI/AbaR system in A. baumannii. This review focuses on QS regulatory mechanisms in ESKAPE pathogens and discusses the novel approaches to target QS-associated virulence and biofilm formation. A review of the literature on QS signaling pathways, biofilm regulation, and anti-QS therapies was performed with special focus on combating strategies like plant-derived phytochemicals, synthetic QS inhibitors, enzymatic quorum quenching, probiotics, and combinations of QS-targeted agents with conventional antibiotics. QS systems are involved in virulence regulation, adhesion, biofilm maturation, and bacterial persistence. Plant-based compounds such as flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and polyphenols have been shown to have potential to interfere with QS-related processes. Synthetic inhibitors, quorum-quenching enzymes, probiotics, and antibiotic combination strategies are also promising approaches. By integrating QS regulation with virulence, biofilm biology, and antimicrobial response across ESKAPE pathogens, this review provides a comparative framework to guide future target prioritization, diagnostic development, and evaluation of adjunctive anti-virulence strategies. Mechanistic validation, standardized cross-pathogen comparisons, and long-term resistance-evolution studies are needed to establish the therapeutic readiness and clinical value of these approaches.

title: In vitro antibacterial and antibiofilm activity of phycocyanin against Klebsiella pneumoniae: effects on growth kinetics and antibiotic susceptibility
abstract: The increasing clinical burden of antimicrobial-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, together with its capacity for biofilm formation and persistence, has intensified the search for alternative and adjunctive antimicrobial strategies. Phycocyanin is a cyanobacteria-derived phycobiliprotein with emerging biological and antimicrobial properties; however, its activity against K. pneumoniae, particularly across planktonic, biofilm, and antibiotic-response phenotypes, remains insufficiently characterized. Klebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 700,603 was used as the experimental strain, and phycocyanin obtained from Sigma was evaluated for antibacterial and antibiofilm activity. Minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) were determined by broth microdilution and subsequent subculture, respectively. Bacterial growth kinetics were monitored for 72 h under sub-inhibitory phycocyanin exposure, while direct antibacterial activity was evaluated using an agar well diffusion assay. Biofilm formation was assessed using the crystal violet microtiter-plate method. Changes in antibiotic inhibition-zone diameters following sub-inhibitory phycocyanin exposure were evaluated using ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and imipenem. All experiments were performed in triplicate. Phycocyanin exhibited measurable antibacterial activity against K. pneumoniae, with MIC and MBC values of 10 and 20 mg/mL, respectively. Growth-kinetic analysis showed comparable bacterial growth during the initial hours, followed by sustained attenuation of growth in phycocyanin-exposed cultures from approximately 6 h onward. In the agar well diffusion assay, inhibition-zone diameters increased in a concentration-dependent manner, from approximately 7 mm at the lowest tested amount to 12 mm at the highest. Phycocyanin also inhibited biofilm formation in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximum inhibition reaching 41.3% at the highest tested concentration. Following sub-inhibitory phycocyanin exposure, increased inhibition-zone diameters were observed for ampicillin, ceftriaxone, and imipenem, with the greatest changes generally occurring after 24 h of exposure. Phycocyanin demonstrated antibacterial and concentration-dependent antibiofilm activity against K. pneumoniae ATCC 700,603 and altered the bacterial antibiotic-response phenotype following sub-inhibitory exposure. The observed effects on bacterial growth, biofilm formation, and antibiotic inhibition-zone diameters suggest that phycocyanin may have potential as an adjunctive antimicrobial or antibiofilm agent. However, these findings do not establish pharmacodynamic synergy or reversal of antimicrobial resistance. Further studies using quantitative combination assays, resistant clinical isolates, mechanistic approaches, and in vivo models are required to determine the translational relevance of these effects.

title: Transmission risk and mechanism of antibiotic resistance genes driven by glacier melt: Insight from Asian water tower to global significance
abstract: Accelerated glacier melt due to climate change is increasingly releasing sequestered antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). However, ARG transmission risk and driven mechanisms that are associated with glacier retreat remain poorly understood. We employed genome-resolved metagenomics along a 246.5 km sampling transect spanning two distinct hydrological seasons and multiple habitats to track the dissemination of ARGs along the hydrological continuum of the Kuoqionggangri Glacier on Tibetan Plateau. Our results demonstrate that hydrological connectivity facilitates the physical transport of antibiotic resistant bacteria. Specific microbial lineages, particularly pathogenic Ralstonia pickettii were traced continuously from glacial sources to downstream rivers, disseminating both ARGs and virulence factors. Beyond host-mediated transport, glacier-derived ARGs can spread into downstream indigenous microbial communities via horizontal gene transfer. Genomic evidence confirmed that sulfonamide and β-lactam determinants transfer across taxonomic boundaries, disseminating from upstream environmental taxa (e.g., Novosphingobium) into downstream opportunistic pathogens. Finally, integrating 156 global glacier metagenomes revealed that the Tibetan Plateau yields an exceptionally high absolute ARG concentration (8.85 ± 0.07 log10 copies/L). Surpassing > 99% of the surveyed regions globally, the sheer magnitude of this genetic discharge identifies glacial melt as a critical emission hotspot, overwhelming downstream aquatic systems with severe ecological resistance risks.

title: The origin of Group B Streptococcus in Australian dogs, cats and cows
abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae, known in human medicine as Group B Streptococcus (GBS), affects numerous animal species, including dairy cattle and companion animals such as dogs and cats. In cattle, where GBS is a common cause of mastitis, host-specialist and host-generalist clades have been detected, whereas data on the origin of companion animal GBS is limited and somewhat contradictory. Here, we analyse a collection of 39 animal GBS isolates from Australia. Based on core genome analysis, the population composition matches the globally observed pattern of occurrence of host-specialist and host-generalist GBS in cattle, represented here by clonal complex 61/67 and sequence type (ST) 23, respectively, and host-generalist GBS in companion animals belonging to multiple sequence types and serotypes. Accessory genome analysis identifies non-exclusive but statistically significant and positive associations between the lactose operon and bovine isolates, and between the scpB gene or antimicrobial resistance genes and companion animal isolates. Proviral regions were detected in all isolates, whereby some phages or phage-inducible chromosomal islands (PICI) were associated with specific sequence types, e.g., phage E2 with ST67 from cattle and phage F2 with ST19 from companion animals. In agreement with results from Europe, our data suggest that GBS infections in dogs and cats are potentially derived from humans and may represent cases of reverse zoonosis.

title: Anthraquinone-enriched fraction of Rheum australe D. Don by Bioassay-guided fractionation and synergistic interaction with tetracycline against Bacterial pathogens
abstract: Rheum australe is an important medicinal herb known as Himalayan rhubarb. Traditionally used in Ayurveda and Tibetan medicine to treat diabetes, diarrhoea, hypertension, obesity, wounds, backache & gastrointestinal diseases. The current study is focused on studying the antibacterial and synergistic potential of the anthraquinone-enriched fraction of R. australe in combination with conventional antibiotics. The extract of R. australe was prepared using 70% ethanol with a Soxhlet apparatus, and Bioassay guided fractionation was done. Broth microdilution methods determined antibacterial and Synergistic activity of crude extracts and subfractions. Phytoconstituents were identified by LC-MS, and molecular docking was done to study the interaction with penicillin-binding protein 3, and docking-predicted potential interacting Phytoconstituents were quantified by HPLC. The extraction yield of the hydroalcoholic extract was recorded as 40.66 ± 3.05%. The chloroform subfraction showed the strongest antibacterial activity among all the subfractions against MRSA (64 μg/ mL), S. aureus (16 μg/mL) &P. aeruginosa (8 μg/mL) mL, and also the strongest synergistic activity with tetracycline against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) (FICI 0.19-0.5), Staphylococcus aureus (FICI 0.0312-0.125), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (FICI 0.125-0.375). Six phytoconstituents (piceatannol, chrysophanol, rhein, aloe-emodin, physcion & emodin) were identified by LC-MS. Molecular docking and MD simulation data revealed that among all the phytoconstituents, aloe-emodin, chrysophanol, emodin, & rhein indicated favourable interactions. HPLC analysis showed that these four phytoconstituents were enriched in the chloroform subfraction. The current study suggests that the chloroform subfraction enriched in anthraquinones exhibits strong antibacterial activity and synergistic activity in combination with tetracycline, and the synergistic mechanism of the combination remains to be established.

title: Combating drug-resistant Aeromonas veronii: Multiomics revealed the antibacterial mechanism of resveratrol
abstract: , widely distributed in aquatic ecosystems, is a prevalent fish pathogen and can cause human infections via contaminated aquatic products, polluted water contact, or tainted food consumption. Escalating antibiotic resistance instrains highlights an urgent need for alternative natural antimicrobial agents. This study investigated resveratrol's antibacterial mechanisms againstand evaluated its protective efficacy in hybrid sturgeon. Resveratrol exhibited strong activity [minimum inhibitory concentration: 128 microgram per milliliter (μg/ml), minimum bactericidal concentration: 256 μg/ml], disrupting cell wall/membrane integrity, inducing reactive oxygen species accumulation, inhibiting adenosine 5'-triphosphate synthesis, and down-regulating key metabolic pathways via transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses. In the sturgeon infection model, resveratrol-nanoemulsion notably improved survival, reduced tissue bacterial loads, mitigated oxidative stress and inflammation, and restored intestinal barrier function. These findings confirm resveratrol as a promising antibiotic alternative against, with nanoemulsion formulation enhancing its therapeutic efficacy.

title: Occurrence and Antimicrobial Resistance Profiles of ESBL-Producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae from Poultry Stool and Raw Meat in Rural and Urban Burkina Faso
abstract: Livestock contributes substantially to global food systems and livelihoods, particularly in low-income countries such as Burkina Faso. However, intensified poultry production has been associated with increased antibiotic use and the emergence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). This study assessed the occurrence and antimicrobial resistance profiles of extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producingandisolated from poultry stool and raw meat samples collected in rural and urban areas of Burkina Faso. This cross-sectional study was conducted between February 2022 and December 2024 in Ouagadougou and Nouna. A total of 374 samples were collected, and the isolates were identified using biochemical testing and the VITEK 2 Compact system. ESBL production was confirmed using the combined-disk method according to EUCAST, 2022 guidelines. ESBL-producingandwere detected in 70 (18.7%; 95% CI: 15.0-23.1) and 25 (6.7%; 95% CI: 4.5-9.8) samples, respectively. Among poultry stool samples, ESBL-producingwere detected at similar frequencies in Ouagadougou and Nouna (Holm-adjusted= 0.250), whereas ESBL-producingwere detected significantly more frequently in Ouagadougou (Holm-adjusted= 0.004).showed high resistance to ampicillin (100%), tetracycline (90.0%), cefuroxime (84.3%), and ceftriaxone (81.4%). Allisolates were resistant to ampicillin, tetracycline, cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, and cotrimoxazole (100% each). Multidrug resistance was observed in 98.6% ofand 100% ofisolates. The detection of these organisms in the poultry production system and raw meat highlights the potential risk of foodborne transmission to humans. These findings underscore the need for improved antimicrobial stewardship, enhanced hygiene during slaughter and processing, and strengthened One Health surveillance strategies.

title: Investigating the multifaceted mechanism of hinokitiol: membrane perturbation and attenuation of quorum sensing-regulated virulence in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has become a major global public health threat due to excessive use of antibiotics, requiring urgent attention to combat multidrug-resistant bacterial strains. In this context, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a clinically important opportunistic microbe, is widely known for causing persistent nosocomial infections due to its ability to form biofilms and secrete multiple quorum sensing (QS)-associated virulence factors. QS is a density-dependent communication system in bacteria that controls biofilm formation and pathogenic potential. Moreover, biofilm provides physical protection to the embedded bacteria from unfavorable conditions like chemicals, antimicrobial agents, pH, temperature, and UV light. In this study, we evaluated hinokitiol (HT) for its antimicrobial, anti-QS, and anti-biofilm activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We also explored the underlying mechanism of action responsible for its growth and QS inhibition. Hinokitiol disrupted the membrane integrity and respiratory chain activity of bacteria at 50 and 100 µg/mL concentrations. In addition, it hinders biofilm formation at sub-inhibitory doses, which was confirmed by crystal violet assay, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and fluorescence microscopy. Furthermore, qRT-PCR analysis showed that all four QS-related genes were downregulated in the presence of hinokitiol. Cytotoxicity analysis revealed that it shows dose-dependent toxicity towards mammalian cell lines, while lower concentrations (less than 25 µg/mL) exhibited no significant toxicity towards L6 cells even after prolonged exposure. These findings indicate that hinokitiol is a promising candidate to combat P. aeruginosa-associated infections.

title: Genomic Profiling of the Virulence Potential and Antimicrobial Resistance of Shiga Toxin-Producing Escherichia coli from Surface Water and Animal Sources
abstract: The aim of this work was to characterize the pathogenic potential of Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) circulating in environmental and animal reservoirs. To achieve this, 225 genomes were analyzed: four genomes were obtained from bovine mastitis isolates, and 221 were obtained from the NCBI Pathogen Detection database originating from surface water and animal fecal samples. All genomes were analyzed to identify virulence-associated factors and antimicrobial resistance profiles in strains collected from surface water and animal samples. Virulence analysis revealed that stx1 and stx2 were detected in 32% and 44% of isolates, respectively. Environmental genomes frequently carried adhesion and LEE-associated genes, while mastitis isolates lacked these markers but exhibited enriched iron uptake systems and hemolysins, indicating niche-specific virulence repertoires. Resistance analysis identified 105 genes that contribute to antimicrobial resistance against multiple antibiotic families, including beta-lactams, quinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and polymyxins. Phylogenetic analysis classified the strains mainly into phylogroups B1 (63.56%) and E (28%), and serotyping identified 41 serotypes, with O157:H7 being the most common (25.33%). MLST revealed 46 STs, with ST11 being the predominant one in animal fecal isolates. Overall, the data indicate a genetically diverse STEC population, with shared lineages among water, feces, and mastitis, as well as combined virulence and multidrug resistance profiles. This supports the need to incorporate genomic surveillance in environmental and livestock reservoirs to anticipate and mitigate the risks of transmission to the human population.

title: Molecular characteristics of Group B Streptococcus isolates from Daqing, Heilongjiang Province, China
abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus, GBS) is an important opportunistic pathogen associated with invasive infections in neonates, pregnant women, and immunocompromised adults, while increasing antimicrobial resistance poses challenges for clinical management. This study investigated the distribution, antimicrobial susceptibility, and molecular characteristics of GBS isolates collected from a tertiary hospital in Daqing, northeastern China. A total of 1,040 non-duplicate GBS isolates collected from outpatients and inpatients between 2020 and 2025 were analysed for specimen distribution and antimicrobial susceptibility. Molecular characterization was performed on 118 archived isolates using multiplex PCR for capsular serotypes, antimicrobial resistance genes, and virulence genes, together with the D-test for macrolide resistance phenotypes. The GBS carriage rate among women in late pregnancy was 6.0% (397/6,669). All isolates were susceptible to penicillin, ampicillin, vancomycin, linezolid, and tigecycline, while the resistance rates to erythromycin, clindamycin and levofloxacin were 93.2, 78, and 66.1%, respectively. Among the 118 characterised isolates, serotype Ib predominated (74.6%), followed by serotypes III (15.3%) and Ia (10.2%). The ermB (83.9%) and ermC (53.4%) genes were the predominant macrolide resistance determinants, and the constitutive MLSB (cMLSB) phenotype was the most common macrolide resistance phenotype (73.7%). These findings provide regional data on the antimicrobial susceptibility and molecular characteristics of GBS in northeastern China.

title: Recombinant outer-membrane vesicles (OMVs) from Salmonella Enteritidis as multivalent candidate vaccines for enteric fevers and invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella infections
abstract: Invasive non-typhoidal(iNTS) infections, typhoid, and paratyphoid fever are major global health burdens, particularly considering increasing antimicrobial resistance. These diseases often colocalize geographically, making broadly protective multivalent vaccines highly desirable. Multicomponent vaccine candidates are currently being developed to achieve protection against multiple systemicdiseases.The aim of this study was to create a vaccine candidate against iNTS and typhoid fever consisting of bacterial outer-membrane vesicles (OMVs) expressing simultaneously multiple key immunogenic antigens on their membrane surface.The abequose synthase () gene was inserted intoEnteritidis to achieve expression of the O:4 surface polysaccharide antigen, alongside the naturally expressed O:9 antigen. The Vi polysaccharide was expressed using a plasmid containing theoperon. Reactogenicity of lipopolysaccharide molecules was reduced by deleting theandgenes to alter Lipid A acylation. Thegene was deleted to increase the yield of OMVs by the mutant bacteria. Immunization of mice with the O:4, O:9, and Vi-expressing OMVs resulted in antibody responses against all three target antigens and reduced bacterial burdens in the livers and spleens of the animals after challenging with virulentTyphimurium andEnteritidis.

title: Bridging generalizability and reproducibility in machine learning-based antimicrobial resistance prediction
abstract: The rapid growth of whole-genome sequencing and machine learning (ML) has led to a multitude of methods for predicting antimicrobial resistance (AMR) from bacterial genomic data. Despite increasingly high reported predictive performance, substantial differences in data sets, phenotype definitions, genomic preprocessing, evaluation strategies, and validation procedures make it difficult to determine whether models will perform reliably beyond the data on which they were developed. In machine learning, this problem is generally framed in terms of generalizability: the ability of a model to maintain performance when applied to previously unseen data. In microbiology, many of the same considerations ultimately manifest as a problem of reproducibility. In this review, we provide a brief overview of the fundamental concepts underlying machine learning-based AMR prediction and then examine the factors that affect model generalizability and reproducibility.

title: Annual hospital antibiograms in low- and middle-income countries: far from obsolete, not yet achieved
Innovative β-lactams and β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations against carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales
abstract: SUMMARYThe global dissemination of carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE) represents one of the most pressing threats to modern antimicrobial therapy. The rapid worldwide expansion of these organisms has been driven by the emergence and successful dissemination of diverse carbapenemases belonging to Ambler classes A, B, and D, including KPC, OXA-48-like, and metallo-β-lactamases, such as NDM, VIM, and IMP. These enzymes severely compromise the activity of carbapenems, historically considered the cornerstone for treatment of severe infections caused by multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria. In response to this growing challenge, substantial efforts in antibiotic discovery have led to the development of several novel β-lactams and β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations specifically designed to restore activity against carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE). This review provides a comprehensive microbiological overview of recently approved and investigational agents targeting CPE. We examine the structural and mechanistic features of key therapeutic options, including cefiderocol and multiple β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations incorporating classical penicillin-based sulfone derivatives, diazabicyclooctanes, and cyclic boronates. Particular attention is given to the biochemical properties and inhibitory spectra of β-lactamase inhibitors, as well as the antimicrobial activity of novel β-lactams and β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations against both isogenic strains and large collections of clinical Enterobacterales isolates. In addition, we discuss the emerging resistance mechanisms that may compromise the clinical effectiveness of these agents. Understanding the mechanistic basis of both activity and resistance is essential to guide their optimal therapeutic positioning and to inform the next generation of antimicrobial development aimed at combating the ongoing threat of CRE.

title: Draft genome sequences of four Escherichia coli strains from lake water in Dhaka, Bangladesh
abstract: The draft genomes of four environmentalstrains reveal potentially pathogenic strains, along with mobile genetic elements, antibiotic resistance genes, and numerous prophage regions, suggesting genetically diversepopulations in Bangladesh's freshwater environments.

title: Off-panel resistance determinants in a high-resistance setting: comparative evaluation of syndromic multiplex PCR, metagenomic sequencing, and phenotypic AST in bloodstream infections
abstract: Rapid syndromic molecular panels substantially reduce turnaround time for bloodstream infection diagnosis by identifying common pathogens and selected antimicrobial resistance determinants directly from positive blood cultures. However, their fixed target repertoires may limit diagnostic coverage in settings with diverse endemic resistance mechanisms and clinically relevant off-panel organisms. This retrospective comparative diagnostic study evaluated direct-from-positive-blood-culture metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS), the BioFire Blood Culture Identification 2 (BCID2) panel, and routine microbiological methods across 165 positive blood-culture episodes from 145 patients at a tertiary-care center with a high burden of antimicrobial resistance. Complete recovery of the routine-culture organism set was achieved in 155/165 episodes (93.9%) by mNGS and 142/165 (86.1%) by BCID2. Among 23 episodes with incomplete routine-set recovery by BCID2, mNGS restored complete coverage in 18 (78.3%). For meropenem resistance, sensitivity was numerically higher with mNGS than with BCID2 (90.0% versus 75.0%), whereas ceftriaxone-resistance sensitivity among Enterobacterales was numerically higher with BCID2 (97.5% versus 85.0%); neither paired difference was statistically significant. BCID2 meropenem very major errors were concentrated among non-fermenting gram-negative organisms, particularly, and were frequently associated with off-paneldetected by mNGS. Overall, targeted syndromic testing and mNGS demonstrated complementary diagnostic performance, with mNGS extending organism and resistance-mechanism coverage beyond predefined molecular targets, while phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing remained necessary for definitive susceptibility assessment.IMPORTANCERapid molecular blood-culture panels provide clinically actionable results, but are inherently restricted to predefined pathogen and resistance targets. This limitation is particularly relevant in regions where local antimicrobial resistance epidemiology includes mechanisms not represented within commercial panel repertoires. In this study, metagenomic sequencing improved recovery of routine-culture organisms and identified off-panel carbapenem resistance determinants underlying several false-susceptible panel results, particularly OXA-23 in. However, broader genomic detection did not consistently improve phenotypic resistance prediction across antimicrobial classes. These findings illustrate that diagnostic breadth and phenotypic predictive accuracy are distinct attributes and support the use of metagenomic sequencing as a complementary approach to rapid targeted testing and conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing.

title: Draft genome sequences of Vibrio cholerae C6706 isolates evolved under erythromycin and tetracycline selection
abstract: We report draft genome sequences of sixC6706 isolates evolvedto an eightfold increase in tetracycline or erythromycin MIC, with three independent lineages per antibiotic. Assemblies comprised 110 to 130 contigs totaling 4.01 to 4.02 Mb, each estimated 100% complete by CheckM2.

title: Mycoplasma genitalium extracellular vesicles and the P140 adhesin carboxyl region as high-fidelity antigens for improved serodiagnosis
abstract: () is an important etiological agent of sexually transmitted infections that has emerged as a global health threat. Despite its clinical importance, accurate serodiagnosis remains challenging due to high cross-reactivity caused by non-specific proteins.
