To address this limitation, we optimizedgrowth in a serum-free minimal medium to characterize the biogenesis and diagnostic applications of-secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs). We demonstrate thatgenerates EVs that retain immunodominant proteins, specifically the key adhesins P140 and P110. From an initial cohort of 1,608 women (12.5%positive), we selected a longitudinal sub-study population, including 24 women who were PCR-positive at enrollment and a control group of 14 individuals who remained-negative across three visits, each spaced approximately 6 months apart. Comparative ELISA and immunoblotting using sera from-infected and uninfected individuals revealed that the EV-associated antigens provide superior diagnostic discrimination over conventional total-cell lysates and lipid-associated membrane protein extracts. Notably, EV-associated antigens lack common non-specific proteins, such as immunoglobulin-binding protein, MG281. Functional characterization using full-length and truncated P140 variants in cell-based ELISAs with human cervical epithelial cells identified the C-terminal region (P140-C) as the primary host-cell-interacting domain. In addition, this specific region induces an epitope-restricted antibody response in infected individuals. Within the longitudinal clinical cohort, high anti-P140-C antibody titers correlated with a trend towardclearance, suggesting potential prognostic utility despite lacking statistical significance. Collectively, these results establishEVs as a high-fidelity antigenic source and identify P140-C as a promising candidate for the development of next-generation serological assays. Serodiagnosis of(Mg) faces significant challenges, especially in the context of emerging antimicrobial resistance and asymptomatic infections. This study introduces-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) as a source of refined antigens for serodiagnosis. By isolating the P140 C-terminal region, we identified a highly specific marker that overcomes antigenic variation, reduces cross-reactivity, and offers a candidate antigen that may warrant evaluation as a marker of infection clearance. By leveraging bacterial EVs as a source of purified diagnostic antigen, our findings offer a framework with broader implications for other antigenically complex pathogens.

title: Draft genome sequence of Escherichia coli SAU_MI_1GVS2 isolated from a goat vaginal swab in Dhaka, Bangladesh
abstract: We describe the draft genome sequence ofSAU_MI_1GVS2, isolated from a goat vaginal swab in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Sequencing with the Illumina NextSeq platform generated a 4.98 Mb genome with 4,619 coding sequences, including genes associated with putative antibiotic resistance and virulence.

title: Pseudomonas sediminis CRE-TB-54 carries tmexCD3-toprJ3 in a novel chromosomal region
abstract: The emergence of tmexCD-toprJ, coding for a transmissible multidrug resistance efflux pump of the resistance-nodulation-division (RND) family has compromised the usefulness of tigecycline in the treatment of infections caused by multidrug resistant Gram-negative bacteria. Here, we describe the presence of tmexCD3-toprJ3 in a novel chromosomal context in Pseudomonas sediminis CRE-TB-54 isolated from a toilet in a university dormitory in southwestern Nigeria. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole genome sequencing showed that CRE-TB-54 displayed intermediate level resistance to tigecycline and haboured multiple antibiotic resistance genes, including tmexCD3-toprJ3 flanked upstream and downstream by genetic structures not previously reported in association with tmexCD-toprJ. These include insertion sequences IS4 and IS30, and the metal resistance gene czcD upstream, the prophage integrase IntA, the competence associated DNA binding protein gene comEA, and the double stranded DNA repair and homologous recombination gene cluster recBCD downstream. These results provide new insight into the genetic structures surrounding the tmexCD-toprJ cluster and raises concern about toilets as a potential environmental reservoir of bacteria carrying this clinically important gene in a resource-limited setting where tigecycline is not currently used in human or animals.

title: Genomic analysis of extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from a dog with a severe episode of self-trauma and urinary tract infection
abstract: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacterales are emerging pathogens of major importance in veterinary medicine. This study describes the clinical, microbiological, and genomic characteristics of ESBL-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae isolated from a dog with paraparesis and concurrent pyelonephritis, chronic cystitis, and a self-traumatized limb lesion. A 12-year-old mixed-breed female dog underwent repeated antimicrobial therapy during hospitalization. Urine obtained by cystocentesis and wound samples were cultured, and ESBL-producing strains were characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing and whole-genome sequence-based analysis. CTX-M-55-producing E. coli sequence type (ST) 457, phylogroup F, O11:H25, and fimH145, was recovered from urine and wound samples, while the wound sample also yielded a CTX-M-15- and SHV-2-producing K. pneumoniae ST39, KL149:OL2α.2. The two closely related E. coli strains differed by 96 single nucleotide polymorphisms, despite sharing the same ST, resistome, plasmid replicons, and virulence profile. ESBL-positive strains carried multiple virulence genes, with the E. coli strains classified as extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli strains. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of ESBL-producing K. pneumoniae ST39 in an animal in Brazil. The co-occurrence of ESBL-producing E. coli ST457 and K. pneumoniae ST39 in the same dog highlights the potential for companion animals to harbor clinically relevant multidrug-resistant lineages and reinforces the need for continuous antimicrobial resistance monitoring and antimicrobial stewardship in this sector.

title: Comparative genomic and resistome analysis of Citrobacter koseri: first genome report from Egypt
abstract: Citrobacter koseri is increasingly implicated in healthcare- and community-associated infections, with multidrug-resistant (MDR) strains posing a growing clinical concern. However, its population structure and resistome dynamics remain incompletely understood. Here, we report the first draft genome sequence of an MDR C. koseri isolate (DFU32) from Egypt, recovered from a patient with a diabetic foot ulcer (DFU). We also present a comparative genomic and resistome analysis of 518 publicly available C. koseri genomes available at the time of the study. The isolate exhibited resistance to multiple antimicrobial classes, including β-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, and sulfonamides, as well as tigecycline and colistin. MLST assigned DFU32 to sequence type (ST) 1172. Genomic analysis identified 21 antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes, including multiple β-lactamases (bla, bla, bla, bla, and bla) and aminoglycoside resistance determinants, including armA. Colistin resistance was associated with the presence of a PhoQ V381I substitution. Comparative analysis of 518 publicly available genomes revealed 140 unique AMR genes across the species, with 73.6% of genomes carrying acquired resistance determinants. The population comprised two major lineages, blaand bla, with the MAL lineage, particularly MAL-2, carrying significantly more AMR genes. Carbapenemase genes were identified in 29.1% of genomes and were distributed across nearly half of the detected STs, with blavariants predominating. Mobilized colistin resistance (mcr) genes were detected in 2.5% of genomes. Both carbapenemase and mcr genes were predominantly located on plasmid-associated contigs. Notably, chromosomal integration events were observed. These included mcr-9.1, which was associated with IS26 and IS903B, and bla, which was embedded within an IS26-bracketed transposon (IS26-recA-ISKpn27-bla-ISKpn6-IS26) in novel STs. These findings underscore the genomic plasticity of C. koseri and the potential for stable, plasmid-independent maintenance of colistin and carbapenem resistance. Among the identified STs, ST690 displayed a particularly high resistance gene load, including carbapenemase and mcr genes, suggesting that it may represent a high-risk lineage. This study provides the first genome-based characterization of an MDR C. koseri isolate from Egypt. The results highlight the potential genetic mobility and global spread of AMR determinants in this emerging pathogen. Notably, the studied isolate was recovered from DFU, underscoring the increasing clinical relevance of C. koseri in chronic wound infections.

title: In silico identification of drug compounds to arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase of Proteus mirabilis to combat its antibiotic resistance using an integrated bioinformatics: subtractive proteomics, molecular docking, MD simulation and DFT studies
abstract: Proteus mirabilis is a major opportunistic Gram-negative pathogen causing complicated urinary tract infections (UTIs), particularly in catheterized patients. Although several antibiotics, including streptomycin, erythromycin, and sparfloxacin, remain effective against some infections, the growing spread of multidrug-resistant P. mirabilis strains has created an urgent need to identify new therapeutic targets and treatment options. Using a subtractive proteomics approach, this study identified potential therapeutic targets in P. mirabilis. Among the 417 essential pathogen-specific proteins, 11 were identified as druggable, virulence-associated, and antibiotic resistance-related proteins, making them promising novel therapeutic targets against P. mirabilis. Among them, nine are enzymatic proteins involved in crucial biological pathways such as glycan and amino acid biosynthesis, energy metabolism, cellular signaling, and genetic information processing. The protein-protein interactions (PPIs) and hub gene analysis revealed arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase (API) as a primary target; structure-guided virtual screening identified five hits, ferric derisomaltose, hyaluronic acid, acarbose, rutin, and dihydrostreptomycin that exhibit binding affinities ranging from -13.540 to -10.616 kcal/mol with P. mirabilis arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase (PmAPI), suggesting their potential as anti-P. mirabilis agents towards infectious disease control. The density functional theory (DFT) studies and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations interaction analysis on PmAPI with potent hits clearly showed reactivity of the hits and stable binding with PmAPI during the 500-ns MD simulation.

title: Influenza vaccination in people with diabetes mellitus: Clinical rationale, current evidence, and implementation challenges
abstract: People with diabetes mellitus (DM) are at increased risk of hospitalisation, complications, and mortality from influenza due to immune dysfunction, metabolic imbalance, and a higher incidence of cardiovascular events. This narrative review, targeted at clinical practice in Spain, summarises recent evidence on diabetes and influenza vaccination and explores barriers to its implementation. Evidence shows that annual vaccination in people with DM reduces hospitalisations, cardiovascular events, and mortality, particularly in those aged ≥ 60 years or with comorbidities; higher-immunogenicity formulations (high-dose or adjuvanted) may provide an additional benefit in these populations. In addition, coadministration with other adult vaccines is feasible. Person-centred recommendations for endocrinology and general practice are proposed to improve suboptimal coverage. Influenza vaccination is cost-effective and may help reduce inappropriate antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance in this population.

title: Global Genomic Analysis of Antimicrobial Resistance in Streptococcus pyogenes
abstract: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus, GAS) is a major global pathogen. While macrolide resistance has been studied, large-scale analyses of overall antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in GAS across geographic datasets remain limited. This study aimed to comprehensively investigate AMR in GAS over more than a century. A total of 47,689 high-quality S. pyogenes genomes from 59 countries, collected between 1900 and 2025 (predominantly post-1990), underwent quality control. Multilocus sequence typing and in silico prediction of AMR determinants using AMRFinderPlus v4.2.5 were performed. Temporal trends were analyzed via quasibinomial regression. Phenotypic susceptibility data from 310 isolates were interpreted using CLSI 2023 breakpoints. GAS showed high genomic conservation (mean genome size, ∼1.81 Mb; ∼1,705 coding sequences). The non-macrolide resistome was dominated by tetracycline and aminoglycoside-associated genes, with tet(M) being the most prevalent (20.96%), followed by aph(3')-IIIa (8.50%), sat4 (8.30%), and ant(6)-Ia (7.69%). Overtime, the prevalence of sat4, aph(3')-IIIa, ant(6)-Ia, and tet(M) increased significantly, whereas that of tet(L), tet(O), and pbp2x_P601L declined (P < 0.05). Reduced susceptibility to selected β-lactams (cefuroxime, imipenem, meropenem) was sporadic (3-10%), primarily linked to pbp2x_P601L, whereas penicillin retained near-universal activity (99.7% susceptibility). Typical β-lactamase genes were rare and geographically restricted. Phenotypic resistance was detected for tetracycline (6%) and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (4%), with 13% showing intermediate susceptibility to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. S. pyogenes remains highly susceptible to penicillin and other β-lactams. Resistance is mainly associated with tetracycline and aminoglycoside genes, which show dynamic changes over time due to ongoing selection pressures.

title: Chloroplast genome engineering: Recent advances, pathways towards commercialization and future directions
abstract: Chloroplasts are ideal biofactories because thousands of transgene copies integrated into each plant cell to produce high levels of recombinant proteins and enzymes. Because chloroplast genomes are predominantly maternally inherited, transgenes are generally not transmitted via pollen. Nuclear genome engineering ushered in the GMO revolution for crop protection that mostly required lower levels of transgene expression. Higher level expression and biosafety through gene containment facilitate new applications of GM crops, including production of high-value biopharmaceuticals and enzymes. This review focuses on recent advances in this field, including the first FDA approval of biopharmaceuticals made in plant cells for evaluation in human clinical trials, topical or oral drug delivery, marker free edible plants by removal of antibiotic resistance genes and novel post-translational modifications required to produce functional human proteins. In addition, new tools are discussed to improve DNA delivery, vector free assembly, episomal or integration methods, enhancement of transgene expression through optimization of regulatory sequences, codons, targeted genome editing and other innovations in biomanufacturing. Topical drug delivery using plant cells incorporated into chewing gums to control oral viruses, pathogenic bacteria, or yeast and oral drug delivery with therapeutic proteins made in plant cells to treat diabetes, obesity and cardiopulmonary diseases currently advanced to human clinical trials are discussed. In addition, high-value industrial enzymes for launching new products or to confer valuable agronomic traits or enhance photosynthesis are discussed. Future perspectives section provides examples of biotechnology products anticipated to be launched in the next 3-5 years, with opportunities and anticipated challenges.

title: Re-securitising antimicrobial resistance: how resurgent health security thinking threatens collective action
Evaluating the Effectiveness of Antimicrobial Stewardship Strategies in Residential Aged Care: An Umbrella Review
abstract: To identify, appraise, and synthesize global evidence on the effectiveness of antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) interventions in residential aged care homes (RACHs). An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Systematic review on AMS interventions for those aged 65 and above who resided in RACHs globally. Fifteen reviews (2013-2024) encompassing 66 unique primary studies were included. Six reviews featured meta-analyses. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, searches across major databases, including Scopus and PubMed, were conducted. Study selection, data extraction, and quality appraisal were performed independently by 2 reviewers. AMS interventions were mapped against the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Core Elements of AMS for nursing homes. Quantitative and qualitative data were synthesized alongside available meta-analyses. Multifaceted AMS strategies combining education, clinical guidelines, drug expertise, and audit and feedback were associated with reductions in antimicrobial consumption, infection rates, and urine culture requests. Long-term implementation (up to 60 months) showed decreased antimicrobial resistance among uropathogens. However, interventions demonstrated little to no impact on the appropriateness of antimicrobial selection, hospital admissions, or mortality. Cost-effectiveness data remained limited. Multifaceted AMS interventions are effective in reducing antibiotic use and infection rates in RACHs. Facilities should implement multifaceted strategies, prioritizing education and clinical algorithms. In resource-limited settings, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention framework and the World Health Organization AWaRe book can be adaptively scaled using nurse-led champions to circumvent high costs. Future longitudinal studies must use standardized aged-care metrics, evaluate cost-effectiveness, and address global equity by investigating AMS models in low- and middle-income countries.

title: A Sequentially Disassembling Nanocomposite Hydrogel with Lesion-Triggered Luteolin Release for Multitarget Acne Vulgaris Therapy
abstract: Acne vulgaris (AV) remains challenging to treat due to antibiotic resistance, side effects, and the lack of topical formulations that concomitantly eradicate Cutibacterium acnes, resolve inflammation, and restore redox homeostasis. Here, we report a sequentially pH-disassembling nanocomposite hydrogel (TCL2.16‰@PQ; PQ represents poly(vinyl alcohol)/quaternized chitosan (PVA/QCS)) for comprehensive AV management, in which tannic acid/Cu2+/luteolin metal-phenolic network nanoparticles (TCL NPs) serve as both drug reservoirs and physical crosslinking nodes within PVA/QCS (PQ) matrix. The hydrogel optimally disassembles at pH 6.5, followed by TCL NP disassembly at pH 6.0, enabling microenvironment-triggered release of luteolin preferentially at the AV lesion site (5.0-7.5, 6.35 ± 1.30; healthy individuals: 4.1-5.8). This design enhances skin permeation flux by 1.5-fold compared to TCL NPs alone. Additionally, the hydrogel's shear-thinning and thixotropic properties make it easy to spread and adhere to the skin. In vitro, the hydrogel completely eradicates Cutibacterium acnes and reduces biofilm biomass by 7.6-fold at 0.2 g/mL, polarizes macrophages to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, and scavenges reactive oxygen species through direct radical scavenging and upregulation of SOD/GPx/HO-1. In a murine AV model, the hydrogel achieved complete bacterial eradication and lesion resolution within 14 days, significantly outperforming a commercial metronidazole gel by concurrently reducing inflammation and restoring redox homeostasis. This work establishes a microenvironment-responsive, multitarget nanocomposite platform addressing the core pathogenic factors of AV, presenting a promising alternative to conventional therapies.

title: The Isolation and Characterisation of Antimicrobial Core Histone from Chondrus crispus species
abstract: Histones are classical DNA-binding proteins, rich in cationic amino acids, and recently also reported as effective antimicrobial agents against a range of Gram-negative and Gram-positive pathogens. While histones with antimicrobial functions have been identified in various marine organisms, little is known regarding the identification and characterisation of innate antimicrobial proteins and peptides, including histones, from macroalgae species. This study aimed to develop an isolation and purification protocol for histones by combining in-silico analyses with wet-laboratory techniques to identify and isolate core histones from the red macroalga Chondrus crispus. The antimicrobial properties of the purified core histone were examined against a variety of pathogenic bacteria using both minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and disk diffusion assays. The purification of the core histone fraction was assessed using SDS-PAGE analysis. The findings indicated that the core histone extracted from C. crispus displayed antimicrobial properties against a range of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including Escherichia coli, Staphylococcus aureus, and the marine pathogens Vibrio anguillarum and Yersinia ruckeri. Furthermore, the purified core histone was digested by trypsin into peptides. The resulting peptides exhibited enhanced bacterial inhibition against both E. coli and S. aureus. These results indicate, for the first time, that C. crispus histone proteins and peptides possess antimicrobial activity. In addition to its antimicrobial properties, the purified core histone showed minimal cytotoxic effects when tested in mammalian cells. As a result, the core histone obtained from C. crispus shows potential as a novel antimicrobial candidate, supporting further evaluation across additional mammalian cell types.

title: Comparative genomics and machine learning reveal antimicrobial resistance landscapes, population structures, and geographic signatures of pork-associated Salmonella Derby across major producing countries
abstract: Salmonella Derby is a major pork-associated foodborne pathogen, yet its genomic diversity across pork-producing countries has not been systematically compared. This study aimed to compare antimicrobial resistance (AMR) landscapes, population structures, and geographic genomic signatures. We analyzed all publicly available pork-associated genomes in the National Center for Biotechnology Information Pathogen Detection database (January 2025) from China (n = 235), France (n = 83), Mexico (n = 38), and the United States (n = 109), using co-occurrence and pairwise association analyses, core-genome phylogeny, and a random forest classifier trained on pan-genome gene presence/absence. Chinese isolates carried the most AMR determinants (15.3 per isolate), followed by Mexican (7.6), French (3.5), and American (3.0) isolates; this difference, and most country-associated AMR genes (ARGs), persisted within sequence type 40 (ST40). Moreover, fosA7.3 and tet(A) were hub ARGs in all countries, and in France ARG and virulence gene profiles were almost perfectly partitioned between ST39 and ST40. Phylogenetic analysis resolved two clades separated by 37,107-38,674 core-genome single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs); the dominant subclade was overwhelmingly ST40. One American ST40 isolate differed by only 18-20 SNPs from three French ST40 isolates. The classifier discriminated country with accuracy of 0.93-0.99 across 21 training:testing splits, remaining ≥ 0.96 when closely related isolates (≤ 10 SNPs) were kept in the same partition; an unannotated gene cluster (group 52) and the efflux pump gene acrF were the most informative features. These findings show strong country-level genomic structuring in pork-associated S. Derby, with implications for global surveillance and source attribution.

title: Raman spectra identify vancomycin-resistant phenotypes and their transcriptomic features in Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: is a pathogenic bacterium that has been linked to multiple epidemics of novel antibiotic resistance. Vancomycin is the first-line antibiotic treatment for methicillin-resistant(MRSA) infections; however, various vancomycin-non-susceptible MRSA strains have emerged globally. Rapid assessment of the resistance levels and the underlying molecular profiles is crucial for preventing their spread and for counteracting resistance. Nevertheless, a broad resistance spectrum and diverse genetic alterations have hindered these efforts. Here, we demonstrated that vancomycin resistance levels of various MRSA strains can be determined using dimension-reduced Raman spectra obtained from single cells. Furthermore, transcriptome profiles of different strains can be predicted from these spectra using simple linear regression. This Raman-transcriptome correspondence enables mapping of transcriptomic components onto a dimension-reduced Raman space, allowing for characterization of gene groups associated with different phenotypes. Additionally, single-cell Raman spectroscopy has successfully identified a strain with higher phenotypic heterogeneity, which was subsequently validated by single-cell growth analysis. Overall, our results demonstrate the efficacy of Raman spectroscopy for identifying resistant phenotypes, their associated features for gene expression, and intrapopulation phenotypic heterogeneity. The spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria threatens human health worldwide. Rapid identification of antibiotic resistance and molecular-level features of an infected pathogen is crucial for treating patients and counteracting the emergence and spread of new resistant bacteria. Here, we demonstrate that Raman spectra, measurable by exposing individual cells to a focused laser, can be used to infer the resistance phenotypes and global gene expression profiles of differentstrains. Furthermore, we present a method to visualize transcriptome components using the major axes of the dimension-reduced Raman space linked to important phenotypic features, such as resistance and virulence. This method identifies several gene sets related to crucial phenotypic features of pathogenic bacteria. Our results demonstrate a novel application of spectroscopy in microbiology by enabling the simultaneous identification of resistant and virulent phenotypes, as well as the underlying gene expression features.

title: Metagenomic insights into the avian gut microbiome: novel viruses, antimicrobial resistance, and beyond
abstract: Birds play crucial roles in shaping ecosystems, and their gut microbiomes significantly influence host physiology and pathology. Understanding the composition, functions, and dynamics of avian gut microbiomes is therefore essential. Recent advances in metagenomic and metatranscriptomic sequencing have greatly increased our ability to characterize the avian gut microbiome. This review presents a systematic summary of the current knowledge regarding the composition of the avian gut microbiome as revealed through high-throughput sequencing technologies. It provides a statistical overview of the predominant bacterial and viral taxa present in the gut microbiomes of 195 bird species, revealing a persistent trend toward the discovery of novel viruses, and gives insight into the gene functions of these taxa. Interestingly, in terms of both antimicrobial resistance and multidrug resistance, wild birds harbor a greater diversity of resistance types than poultry. This review also presents a discussion of the relationships of avian life stages and the living conditions of birds with the gut microbiome and highlights practical applications of microbiome regulation in poultry production. Building on this foundation, future research priorities are outlined, such as the study of archaea, fungi, protists, and novel viruses, ways of improving methods to reduce costs and standardize protocols, and the development of more extensive metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data resources. Ultimately, these efforts could provide a holistic understanding of the avian gut microbiome.

title: PCR-amplified blaKPC-2-triggered Cas12a activation coupled with DNA cube-confined Fc reporter cleavage on a Ti(3)C(2)/CsPbBr(3)@PDA@Au/GCE dual-mode ECL/SERS interface
abstract: Rapid and reliable detection of antibiotic resistance genes is essential for guiding antimicrobial therapy and controlling the spread of carbapenem-resistant pathogens. Herein, we developed a PCR amplicon-activated CRISPR/Cas12a-regulated dual-mode electrochemiluminescence/surface-enhanced Raman scattering biosensor for sensitive detection of the blaKPC-2 resistance gene. A specific blaKPC-2 fragment containing the selected TTTG PAM region was amplified by PCR and used as a double-stranded DNA activator for the crRNA/Cas12a complex. After target recognition, activated Cas12a cleaved the Fc-labeled reporter segments integrated into a DNA cube scaffold assembled on the TiC/CsPbBr@PDA@Au nanocomposite interface. In the initial state, Fc was positioned close to the TiC/CsPbBr@PDA@Au-modified GCE surface, resulting in ECL quenching and strong SERS emission. Upon Cas12a-mediated cleavage of the exposed ssDNA reporter segments, Fc-containing fragments were released from the interface, leading to ECL recovery and SERS attenuation. Therefore, the target-induced process enabled an anti-correlated ECL-on/SERS-off signal conversion, and the ratiometric value=/was used for quantitative analysis. The concentration-dependent response was empirically fitted over 10-10copies per µL, whereas the 10copies per µL group exhibited upper-range response compression. Boundary back-calculation indicated that further quantitative validation is required. Blank-response inverse prediction gave a model-dependent response-equivalent concentration of approximately 1.06 copies per µL; Poisson sampling gave a 95% molecular-sampling threshold of approximately 3.0 copies per µL for a 1.0 µL input. Neither descriptor is an experimentally determined detection or quantification limit. The platform also exhibited good selectivity against other resistance genes and non-target bacterial genomic DNA, together with satisfactory repeatability, reproducibility, stability, and acceptable spike-recovery performance in 10% diluted serum as a model biological matrix, providing preliminary evidence of matrix tolerance rather than clinical validation. This work provides a self-calibrated dual-mode strategy for antibiotic resistance gene detection, while further validation using bacterial lysates, extracted bacterial genomic DNA, and clinical bacterial isolates is required before diagnostic application. qPCR supported linear amplification over 10-10copies per µL; endpoint responses remained observable through 10copies per µL, where quantitative resolution was reduced.

title: Evaluating the Impact of Urine Reflex Testing on Antibiotic Prescribing for Urinary Tract Infections
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common indications for outpatient antibiotic prescribing. Despite clinical guidelines promoting appropriate antibiotic use, unnecessary urine cultures and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria continue to contribute to adverse drug reactions and antimicrobial resistance. To improve diagnostic stewardship, Kaiser Permanente Southern California (KPSC) region implemented urinalysis (UA) with reflex to microscopy and urine culture (UC), in which microscopy and culture are automatically performed when predefined UA parameters are positive. This strategy aims to improve diagnostic accuracy and reduce inappropriate antibiotic use. This retrospective, pre- and post-implementation observational study evaluated the impact of urine reflex testing on outpatient antibiotic prescribing for suspected UTI across KPSC. Patients were included if they were KPSC members aged 2 years with either a UA or UC collected between July 1, 2021 and June 30, 2025. Patients who were pregnant, immunocompromised, had an indwelling catheter, or were hospitalized were excluded. Over 3.7 million outpatient encounters were analyzed. Overall antibiotic prescribing within 7 days remained similar (23.2% vs. 23.4%; p<0.0001). However, prescribing was more aligned with culture results, with decreased antibiotic use following negative cultures (25.0% to 23.3%; p<0.0001) and increased use following positive cultures (75.9% to 77.6%; p<0.0001). Antibiotic switched within 7 days of index encounter increased (9.1% to 10.4%; p<0.0001). Diagnostic testing patterns shifted with UA, stand-alone UC, and positive UC decreased, while urine reflex testing increased. Implementation of UA with reflex testing standardized diagnostic workflows and improved alignment of antibiotic prescribing with microbiologic findings.

title: Air pollution is associated with a distinct pathogen spectrum in community-acquired pneumonia: a prospective multicentre cohort study
abstract: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is the leading cause of death due to infection worldwide, with its incidence and disease course influenced by air pollution exposure. Little is known about how air pollution influences microbiological findings in patients with CAP. Patients were recruited from a prospective, multicentre study of CAP (CAPNETZ). Air pollution data were collected at the city level considering data up to one month before inclusion. Associations with sputum pathogen detection and cell counts were tested using generalised linear mixed-effects logistic regression models adjusting for clinical confounders, centre-level heterogeneity and meteorological data. Internal validation was performed using an Ensemble Feature Selection (EFS) approach. Among 4,446 eligible patients with available sputum samples, a potential pathogen was detected in 1,581 patients, while complete sputum-cell-count data were available for 4,014 patients. Detection of Streptococcus pneumoniae was associated with previous higher exposure to sulphur dioxide (SO) (OR 1.75, p = 0.008) and carbon monoxide (CO) (OR 1.57, p = 0.02). Escherichia coli was more frequently detected in patients who were exposed to elevated levels of nitrogen dioxide (NO) (OR 2.75, p = 0.004) and higher temperature (OR 1.51, p = 0.03), whereas increased fine particulate matter (PM) exposure (OR 0.37, p = 0.001) was linked to reduced detection. Furthermore, SOexposure influenced the likelihood of obtaining a diagnostically relevant sputum culture and was associated with higher odds of detecting a high leucocyte count (OR 1.18, p = 0.02). Results were largely corroborated by EFS, particularly for S. pneumoniae and E. coli detection. Exposure to air pollution was associated with a distinct pathogen spectrum in patients with CAP. These findings may have implications for the interpretation of microbiological data in an epidemiological and clinical context and highlight the importance of considering air pollution exposure as a confounding factor. Further validation in cohorts with high-quality environmental, microbiological and antimicrobial resistance data is needed. Registry: German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS), DRKS-ID: DRKS00005274, Registration date: 2013-09-11.

title: Phage-meropenem synergy against multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae biofilms: phenotypic and genomic characterisation of vB_KpnS_Tech
abstract: The increasing prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) Klebsiella pneumoniae and its capacity to form persistent biofilms highlight the need for alternative antimicrobial strategies. This study characterised the lytic bacteriophage vB_KpnS_Tech (PQ859379.1) and evaluated its activity in combination with meropenem against established MDR K. pneumoniae biofilms of different maturities. vB_KpnS_Tech exhibited rapid adsorption, with 98.8% of phage particles adsorbed within 7.5 min, a latent period of approximately 30 min and a mean burst size of approximately 165 PFU per infected cell. The 49,562-bp genome had a GC content of 51.1% and contained 86 predicted coding sequences, including putative holin, endolysin and Rz-like spanin-associated lysis proteins. No recognised antimicrobial-resistance, virulence or lysogeny-associated determinants were detected by the applied genomic screens, and comparative analyses placed vB_KpnS_Tech within the family Drexlerviridae and genus Webervirus, within an existing species-level genomic cluster. Phage-meropenem checkerboard assays demonstrated a clear effect of biofilm maturity on treatment response. Maximum relative biomass reduction reached 66.0% in 24 h biofilms, while the selected combination of 1 × 10⁹ PFU/ml phage and 256 µg/ml meropenem produced reductions of 62.2% and 42.7% in 24 h and 48 h biofilms, respectively. Independent Bliss analysis of biological replicate checkerboards demonstrated synergy in 24 h biofilms, with a mean global score of 10.53 ± 0.53, whereas the interaction in 48 h biofilms was attenuated and remained within the additive/independent range (3.37 ± 0.88). The selected combination reduced recoverable viable bacterial burden by 2.60 and 1.70 log₁₀ CFU/ml relative to untreated endpoints in 24 h and 48 h biofilms, respectively, and reduced viable counts below corresponding pre-treatment baselines. Combination treatment was also associated with the greatest reductions in recoverable EPS-associated carbohydrate, extracellular protein and extracellular nucleic-acid material and retained activity against five additional phage-susceptible MDR K.pneumoniae isolates. Collectively, these findings demonstrate a concentration- and maturity-dependent phage-meropenem interaction and support further evaluation of vB_KpnS_Tech-meropenem combinations against established MDR K.pneumoniae biofilms.

title: Antimicrobial peptides for companion animals: research advances, translational challenges, and opportunities
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a growing global threat to public health, necessitating the development of novel antimicrobial strategies. Companion animals, particularly dogs and cats, are increasingly integrated into human lives, and their close interactions with humans facilitate the transmission of antimicrobial-resistant pathogens. Therefore, the use of contemporary antimicrobials in these animals raises significant concerns for both animal and human health. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), a class of naturally occurring peptides, play a critical role in host innate immunity through dual antimicrobial and immunomodulatory activities. Due to their pleiotropic mechanisms of action and lower selective pressure for resistance, AMPs are emerging as promising alternative candidates to conventional antimicrobials. Notably, accumulating evidence has also highlighted the promising antitumor capacity of AMPs, expanding their therapeutic potential beyond microbial infection control. Despite their potential, research on AMPs in companion animals remains limited, with most available evidence derived from in vitro assays and pre‑clinical in vivo experiments, while well‑controlled clinical studies are sparse. This review overviews recent advances in AMP research in dogs and cats, discusses major challenges in their development, and outlines future directions for their application in veterinary medicine. The adoption of AMPs in small animal practice has the potential to improve animal health while contributing to the mitigation of AMR. Collectively, this review offers new insights into the development of multifunctional novel therapeutic strategies in companion animals.

title: Paper-based colourimetric biosensor for simultaneous detection of UTI-associated nitrite and β-lactamase-mediated resistance using an iodometric method
abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most prevalent bacterial infections worldwide and are increasingly complicated by the emergence of antibiotic resistance, particularly β- lactam resistance. Conventional diagnostic methods for UTI identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing are often labour-intensive and time-consuming and require laboratory infrastructure, thereby restricting their use in resource-limited settings. To address this gap, this study developed a smartphone-assisted, paper-based colourimetric biosensor for the simultaneous detection of UTI-associated nitrite and β-lactamase-mediated antibiotic resistance, integrating two clinically relevant indicators into a low-cost, single platform with smartphone-assisted quantitative readout. The sensing device was fabricated from Whatman Grade-1 filter paper with hydrophobic barriers to form separate detection zones for nitrite and β-lactamase analysis. The nitrite detection zone employed the Griess reaction, while the antibiotic resistance detection zone utilized an agarose- based iodometric system containing penicillin G, iodine, starch, and chitosan- capped silver nanoparticles (AgChNPs). The synthesised AgChNPs were characterised by FT-IR, UV-visible spectroscopy, HRTEM, and zeta potential analysis, confirming successful synthesis. Artificial urine samples were analysed using smartphone-based image acquisition and ImageJ-based intensity quantification. The nitrite detection zone exhibited limits of detection (LoD) and limits of quantification (LoQ) of 0.670 and 2.031 ppm, respectively, while the β-lactamase detection zone showed corresponding values of 0.324 and 0.983 U/mL. The proposed platform offers a rapid, affordable, portable, and integrated approach for simultaneous UTI screening and β-lactamase-mediated antibiotic resistance detection, with potential for point-of-care applications in resource-limited settings.

title: Integrated engineering of antibiotic-marker-free cyanobacterial chassis for enhanced recombinant protein accumulation and intestinal localization
abstract: Engineered cyanobacteria are promising microbial chassis for recombinant protein production and oral delivery, but low intracellular accumulation, expression-associated physiological burden, and residual antibiotic-resistance markers limit their application. Here, we developed an integrated protein-production and marker-removal strategy in Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 and evaluated chromosomal reporter expression in Arthrospira platensis NIES-39. The CpcB-based expression configuration at the native phycocyanin locus resulted in markedly higher mVenus accumulation than free expression at the NSC1 neutral site, accompanied by reduced culture growth and altered photosynthetic characteristics. Incorporation of a tobacco etch virus protease recognition site, together with chromosomal TEV protease expression, enabled partial intracellular cleavage of the fusion protein. Sequential CRISPR-Cpf1 editing and SacB counterselection enabled the removal of targeted antibiotic-resistance cassettes in Synechocystis, as supported by locus-specific PCR and Sanger sequencing. Chromosomal mVenus expression was also established in A. platensis, although the complete marker-removal strategy was not successfully transferred to this host. Under zebrafish-oriented in vitro intestinal conditions, engineered Synechocystis exhibited pronounced structural disruption, whereas A. platensis filaments fragmented more gradually, accompanied by the release of intracellular components. Following zebrafish feeding, reporter-associated fluorescence was detected in the examined intestinal sections at 6 h after administration. Together, these results establish a Synechocystis engineering framework integrating enhanced recombinant protein accumulation, protease-mediated intracellular processing, and targeted antibiotic-marker removal, with complementary assessment of intestinal mVenus-associated fluorescence following oral administration.

title: Genetic code expansion for site-specific encoding of a switchable, intrinsic fluorophore-quencher pair to monitor protein dynamics
abstract: Precisely modifying proteins at multiple sites in their native, folded structures offers unique opportunities to answer molecular and cellular-level biological questions. Here, we present a genetic code expansion strategy for site-specific integration of a fluorophore-quencher pair comprising two non-canonical amino acids-acridonylalanine (Acd) and methyltetrazinyl phenylalanine (Tet)-into a protein expressed in. The Acd and Tet pair requires no post-translational labeling, and quenching can be switched off by bioorthogonal or photochemical reactions of Tet for convenient internal control experiments. Mechanistic studies based on Stern-Volmer quenching, fluorescence lifetime measurements, and "proline ruler" peptides established the distance dependence of quenching. As proof-of-concept, we applied this strategy to study: (1) calmodulin, a calcium-sensing protein, (2) RecA, a DNA damage sensor in bacteria, and (3) LexA, a transcriptional repressor whose activation by RecA governs acquired antibiotic resistance in bacteria. Using these proteins, we demonstrate that dual Acd/Tet labeling provides molecular-level insights into protein dynamics, shows potential for adaptation to high-throughput drug screening, and advances tools for studying protein structure-function relationships.

title: Global change reshapes marine microbial communities, functions and One Health outcomes
abstract: Marine microorganisms underpin primary production, biogeochemical cycling and host-associated symbioses, supporting climate regulation, coastal protection, fisheries and other ecosystem services. Rapid global change, including ocean warming and marine heatwaves, acidification, deoxygenation, eutrophication, pollution and overuse reshape microbial communities and their functions across marine habitats. These changes can alter carbon, nitrogen and sulfur cycles, promote microbialization and harmful algal blooms, disrupt host-microbiome associations and modify pathogen and antimicrobial resistance dynamics, collectively amplifying the ecological and societal impacts of global change. This Review frames marine microbiomes as cross-scale mediators that translate external pressures, including climate change, pollution, eutrophication and habitat degradation, into altered microbial metabolism, biogeochemical fluxes, host-associated health outcomes, ecosystem service consequences and broader One Health risks. We synthesize shared mechanisms and cross-habitat patterns, highlight cases in which microbiome interventions and stewardship could mitigate impacts and/or accelerate recovery, and outline management options ranging from the reduction of local stressors to emerging microbiome stewardship approaches in ecosystem restoration. Building upon this, we outline pathways for embedding marine microbiome science into globally coordinated One Health strategies, operational management protocols and financing frameworks that align economic incentives with long-term ecosystem and public health outcomes.

title: The plasmid arsenal within: Type IV-A CRISPR-Cas systems in Enterobacteriaceae as modulators of resistance and virulence
abstract: The Enterobacteriaceae family, which includes prominent pathogens such as K. pneumoniae, E. coli, and S. enterica, poses a significant global health threat due to the rapid dissemination of multidrug resistance and virulence determinants. Central to this dissemination are conjugative plasmids, which act as vehicles for horizontal gene transfer. Among the myriad defense systems that interact with these mobile genetic elements, the type IV-A CRISPR-Cas system stands out due to its enigmatic nature and unique plasmid-centric biology. Unlike canonical CRISPR-Cas systems that are chromosomal and target bacteriophages, type IV-A systems are predominantly encoded on large, conjugative plasmids, particularly those bearing IncHI1B/IncFIB replicons. This review synthesizes current evidence on the biology of type IV-A systems within Enterobacteriaceae, elucidating their role as mediators of inter-plasmid competition, their paradoxical association with the spread of antibiotic resistance and virulence genes, and their emerging applications as programmable tools. We explore the mechanistic basis for their function as a natural CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) system, the epidemiological landscape of their distribution, and the dual role they play in both constraining and facilitating the dissemination of clinically relevant traits. Finally, we propose ambitious research avenues, including the development of "plasmid-destroying" probiotics, the use of type IV-A systems as epidemiological biosensors, and the exploration of hypotheses concerning their role in mediating bacterial "altruism" or serving as a "genetic memory" of the plasmid "secretoome."

title: In Vitro Activity of Cefiderocol against Carbapenem-Resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Acinetobacter baumannii and the Cefiderocol Resistance Mechanisms
abstract: Extensively drug-resistant and pandrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria, including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, pose a major threat due to limited treatment options and high mortality. Rising prevalence of carbapenem resistance has further complicated therapy, necessitating novel antimicrobial agents. Cefiderocol, a siderophore-conjugated cephalosporin, offers a promising therapeutic option against these multidrug-resistant pathogens. To assess the in vitro activity of cefiderocol and key comparators against carbapenem-resistant Gram-negative bacteria from a Malaysian hospital. A total of 448 non-duplicate carbapenem-resistant bacterial strains collected from the University Malaya Medical Centre diagnostic laboratory from year 2018-2021 were included. Broth microdilution was used for susceptibility testing of cefiderocol and other agents relevant to the respective carbapenem-resistant organisms (CROs), in accordance with CLSI guidelines. Susceptibility was interpreted using CLSI breakpoints, with FDA breakpoints applied for tigecycline. Genotypic detection of antimicrobial resistance-associated genes was performed via polymerase chain reaction. Whole genome sequencing was performed on cefiderocol-resistant isolates for genetic characterisation. Cefiderocol demonstrated the highest susceptibility rate for the tested CROs when compared to other antimicrobial agents. More than 90% of the carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii isolates were susceptible to cefiderocol, whereas 81.2% of carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates were susceptible. Among a total of 22 cefiderocol-resistant isolates, 17 isolates produced NDM-1 and 11 isolates produced PER or VEB ESBL. Cefiderocol remains an effective treatment option for patients infected with CROs. Ongoing surveillance and antibiotic stewardship are essential to monitor the emergence of resistance and preserve the effectiveness of cefiderocol against multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Prior ceftriaxone susceptibility and current nonsusceptibility in paired urinary isolates over time: a retrospective longitudinal cohort study
abstract: To quantify how the association between prior ceftriaxone susceptibility and current nonsusceptibility varies across culture intervals and whether it differs by species concordance or recorded antibiotic exposure between cultures. We conducted a retrospective longitudinal cohort study using the 1999-2024 Antibiotic Resistance Microbiology Dataset. Emergency department-associated urine cultures yielding Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Proteus mirabilis with direct ceftriaxone susceptibility results were paired with the most recent eligible prior culture obtained more than 14 days earlier. Logistic generalised estimating equations adjusted for age group and anonymised gender code estimated marginal standardised probabilities, risk differences, and risk ratios across eight intervals. The analysis included 4,547 culture pairs from 2,993 patients; 654 current isolates (14.4%) were nonsusceptible. At 15-30 days, the adjusted probability of current nonsusceptibility was 92.3% after a prior nonsusceptible result versus 4.7% after a prior susceptible result; at 31-60 days, probabilities were 88.3% versus 3.8%. Adjusted risk differences were 87.6 and 84.4 percentage points, respectively. Beyond 1095 days, probabilities were 22.1% versus 7.3% (risk difference, 14.8 percentage points; risk ratio, 3.01). The susceptibility-by-interval interaction was significant (P < 0.001). The association was stronger in same-species pairs and differed by recorded antibiotic exposure between cultures (both interaction P < 0.001). Prior ceftriaxone susceptibility provided time-dependent, patient-specific information about current nonsusceptibility. Recent prior nonsusceptibility, particularly with species concordance, was associated with a high probability of current nonsusceptibility, although the association attenuated over time.

title: A case-case-control study of cefovecin use and third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Escherichia coli infections in cats
abstract: To determine if cefovecin administration increased the risk of third-generation cephalosporin (3GC)-resistant Escherichia coli infections in cats. In this retrospective case-case-control study, cases were cats with 3GC-susceptible or 3GC-resistant E coli infections at the Cornell University Hospital for Animals from 2009 to 2023; controls were randomly selected from all feline patients seen during the study period. Exposure data were collected via review of medical records. Direct acyclic graph-driven multivariable regression models of each potential exposure were built for each case-control grouping. 36 susceptible cases (3% cefovecin treated), 14 resistant cases (21% cefovecin treated), and 72 controls (6% cefovecin treated) were identified. Resistant cases had a higher proportion of cefovecin use (21%) than susceptible cases (3%) and controls (6%), but case numbers were too low to evaluate whether cefovecin use was associated with either infection type. Most of the cats that received cefovecin (75%) were underdosed. The overall frequency of cefovecin administration was low (7%) compared to previous studies. Cefovecin use was less frequent than previously reported, resulting in too few cases to determine whether cefovecin use is associated with 3GC-resistant E coli infections in cats. The sample size was too small to evaluate association between cefovecin and 3CG resistance. Based on prudent antimicrobial stewardship, veterinarians should limit cefovecin use to cases where oral antimicrobial treatment is impossible and, ideally, its use is supported by antimicrobial susceptibility testing to avoid selecting for antimicrobial resistance in treated cats. When using cefovecin, veterinarians should ensure they are administering the label-recommended 8-mg/kg dose.

title: Current and emerging threats to honey bee health: a One Health perspective on antibiotic pollution
abstract: Pollinators play a critical role in global food production and ecosystem health, yet high losses of essential honey bee colonies have been reported worldwide. Climate change, habitat loss, parasites, pesticides, and poor nutrition are established pollinator threats, whereas environmental antibiotic pollution remains poorly understood. Antibiotic exposure may independently affect bees or interact with these stressors, potentially compounding adverse health effects. Synthetic antibiotic residues and resistance genes enter the environment through the fertilization of soils with antibiotic-containing animal manure, animal wastewater discharge, and airborne antibiotic contamination landing directly on flowers and crops. While the effects of direct antibiotic exposure on honey bees have been studied, the consequences of indirect environmental exposure remain largely unknown. Foraging bees may encounter antibiotic contaminants in the environment, potentially disrupting their gut microbiome, altering behavior and physiology, and increasing susceptibility to pathogens. Contamination of honey bees and their products with antibiotics serve not only as indicators of environmental antibiotic resistance but also as a practical One Health model linking human, animal, and environmental health. Studying honey bee responses to agricultural contaminants provides insight into how antibiotic resistance and environmental stressors can move across ecosystems, affecting both pollinators and the broader public. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the multifactor threats to honey bees and their mitigation strategies, emphasizing the influence of animal production and antibiotic pollution on honey bee health. We highlight knowledge gaps in understanding the transfer of antibiotic resistance from agricultural environments to honey bees to enhance pollinator health and promote long-term ecological resilience.

title: Plasmid-mediated dissemination of antimicrobial resistance among multidrug-resistant bacteria isolated from food-contact surfaces in university cafeterias
abstract: Food-contact surfaces may facilitate the spread of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria in food-service settings. We examined 42 samples (spoons, plates, forks, drinking cups, chopping boards, and washing water; six per cafeteria) from seven university cafeterias in Peshawar, Pakistan. Twenty-seven samples (64.3%) yielded growth: Escherichia coli (8; 29.6%), Staphylococcus aureus (6; 22.2%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (5; 18.5%), Enterobacter cloacae (5; 18.5%), and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (3; 11.1%), identified by biochemical tests and 16 S rRNA sequencing. Chopping boards and washing water were most frequently contaminated. Resistance to β-lactams was common, whereas meropenem remained active against most isolates. Sixteen isolates (59.3%) were multidrug-resistant (MDR) and three (11.1%) were extensively drug-resistant. Among MDR isolates, blaTEM (68.75%) and blaCTX-M (62.5%) were the most frequent of 12 genes screened by PCR, followed by tetA, blaSHV, blaOXA, aac(6')-Ib, qnrA, qnrB, sul1, tetM, blaNDM, and mecA. Eleven of 13 MDR Gram-negative isolates carried plasmids, and seven of these 11 transferred β-lactam resistance to E. coli J53 in filter-mating assays. These findings indicate that cafeteria food-contact surfaces can harbor MDR bacteria with potentially transferable resistance genes, supporting improved sanitation and routine surveillance.

title: Effect of continuous application of pig manure on soil antibiotic resistance genes
abstract: The large-scale application of livestock and poultry manure in protected agriculture is common; however, research on the spread of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) from this practice remains limited. Herein, 16 S and metagenomic sequencing methods were used to investigate the effects of eight consecutive years of pig manure application on tetracycline (TC) antibiotics in protected soil and to evaluate the ecological consequences. In addition, the characteristics of soil ARGs and bacterial diversity were explored, and the potential hosts of ARGs in protected soil and the influence of environmental factors on these potential hosts and ARGs were preliminarily investigated. After 8 years of applying composted pig manure, the total tetracycline residues in the protected soil was as follows: commercial organic fertilizer soil > pig manure soil > rapeseed cake fertilizer soil. Soil enzymes indirectly affect ARG abundance by influencing the microbial community structure. g__unclassified_p__Acidobacteria and g__unclassified_c__Actinomycetia may be the two most important ARG hosts, with a highly significant positive correlation with 32 ARG subtypes. Total nitrogen (TN) and soil organic matter (SOM) significantly promoted the abundance of these two important potential hosts. Nocardioides, g__unclassified_o__Solirubrobacterales, Actinoplanes, and Methyloceanibacter are potential hosts for intI1. TC, Soil urease(S-UE), Soil acid phosphatase(ACP), Soil β-glucosidase(S-β-GC), TN, total phosphorus (TP), and SOM significantly promoted the abundance of potential intI1 hosts. Soil environmental factors collectively accounted for 72.27% of ARG variation, making them the most important factor affecting ARGs. Our research will support manure management in protected agriculture to reduce ARG spread.

title: Repurposing proton pump inhibitors to restore ceftriaxone activity against multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae: phenotypic, molecular, and in silico evidence
abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae has emerged as one of the most clinically significant multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens, with multidrug efflux systems playing a pivotal role in antibiotic resistance and therapeutic failure. This study investigated the contribution of the efflux-associated genes kpnE, kmrA, and kdeA to ceftriaxone resistance and evaluated proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) as efflux pump-targeting adjuvants. Fifty clinical K. pneumoniae isolates were characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, MDR/XDR classification, phenotypic efflux activity assays, molecular detection of efflux-associated genes, kpnE sequencing, quantitative real-time PCR, molecular docking, and ceftriaxone minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) determination in the presence and absence of omeprazole and lansoprazole. MDR and XDR phenotypes were identified in 70% and 18% of isolates, respectively, whereas active efflux was detected in 14% of isolates and was significantly associated with increasing resistance severity. Sequence analysis demonstrated marked conservation of kpnE, with a single D → G amino acid substitution identified in one isolate. Despite this conservation, gene expression analysis revealed substantial isolate-dependent transcriptional responses that were not directly correlated with phenotypic efflux activity, suggesting that transporter efficiency is governed by complex interactions between transcriptional regulation, structural adaptation, and protein functionality rather than gene expression alone. Molecular docking demonstrated favorable binding of both PPIs to KpnE, KmrA, and KdeA, supporting their potential to interfere with efflux-mediated drug extrusion. Consistent with these predictions, combination assays markedly potentiated ceftriaxone activity, reducing MIC values by up to 16,516-fold and restoring ceftriaxone susceptibility in all seven tested efflux-active ceftriaxone-resistant isolates, with omeprazole producing the greatest synergistic effect. Collectively, these findings provide new mechanistic insight into the role of SMR-associated efflux systems in K. pneumoniae antimicrobial resistance and identify proton pump inhibitors, particularly omeprazole, as potential antibiotic adjuvants for restoring β-lactam efficacy against MDR and XDR K. pneumoniae. Further functional and in vivo studies are warranted to determine whether these in vitro findings can be translated into clinically relevant therapeutic applications.

title: Epidemiological and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of Staphylococcus aureus isolated from the nasal cavity of healthcare personnel at a public hospital in Northeastern Brazil: a cross-sectional survey
abstract: Nasal colonization by Staphylococcus aureus among healthcare professionals represents a potential risk for the spread of resistant strains in hospital settings. Thus, this cross-sectional study aimed to determine the prevalence of nasal colonization by S. aureus and to characterize the antimicrobial resistance profile of the isolated strains from professionals working in a public hospital in Caxias, Maranhão, Brazil. This study was carried out from December 2024 to February 2025. A total of 132 professionals working in a public hospital in the state of Maranhão were included. Among the participants, 36 (27.27%) were colonized by S. aureus, and 6 isolates (16.66%) were identified as methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA). High resistance rates were observed to penicillin G and ampicillin (94.4%), as well as to the macrolides erythromycin (83.3%) and azithromycin (77.8%). Resistance to tetracycline was detected in 11.1% of the isolates, with 22.2% showing intermediate susceptibility. All isolates were susceptible to clindamycin, chloramphenicol, and rifampicin. Regarding risk factors, working in two healthcare locations compared to one remained significantly associated with nasal colonization after adjustment (OR = 3.15-3.50; p < 0.05), whereas longer professional experience was identified as a protective factor (OR ranging from 0.11 to 0.17; p < 0.05). These findings demonstrate the circulation of multidrug-resistant S. aureus strains among healthcare professionals and highlight the importance of active surveillance, rational antimicrobial use, and strengthened infection control strategies to reduce the spread of resistant pathogens in hospital environments.

title: Dual-mode biosensing featuring fluorescence and electrochemiluminescence for regional resolution of single-nucleotide variants
abstract: Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) are a critical molecular basis for antibiotic resistance in pathogenic bacteria. However, precise detection of mutant targets remains challenging because they may exist at low abundance and often coexist with wild-type sequences in complex biological matrices. Herein, we report a target-triggered strand displacement reaction that releases two functional DNA strands: one activates the trans-cleavage activity of CRISPR/Cas12a to generate a fluorescent signal, while the other competitively displaces cadmium sulfide quantum dots pre-modified on a gold electrode surface, decreasing the electrochemiluminescence (ECL) signal. The two functional strands hybridize to distinct regions of the probe, enabling the two signaling channels to respond differentially to single-base mismatches at different locations. Taking the response to wild-type targets as a reference, synchronized changes in both signals reflect target concentration. A significant decrease in the fluorescence signal alone, with the ECL signal unchanged, indicates that the mismatch occurs within the fluorescence recognition region, whereupon the unaffected ECL channel may serve for quantification. Conversely, when the ECL signal decreases while the fluorescence signal remains stable, the fluorescence channel may serve for quantification. This design enables a single probe to discriminate between wild-type and mutant targets based on the differential responses of the two signaling channels. Our strategy thus provides a new avenue for single-base nucleic acid detection.

title: Carbapenemase-Producing Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales Among Children in the United States, 2019-2024
abstract: The current epidemiology of carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) among pediatric patients in the United States is poorly described. We assessed trends in pediatric CRE and carbapenemase-producing-CRE (CP-CRE) incidence in the U.S. and characterized recent pediatric CP-CRE cases. We analyzed CRE clinical isolates from patients <18 years submitted to CDC's Antimicrobial Resistance Laboratory Network from January 2019 through December 2024. Annual unadjusted incidence rates for CRE and CP-CRE were estimated overall and by age group for a national convenience sample and an open cohort of 29 states with required CRE isolate submission. Trends were assessed using Poisson regression. For pediatric patients with incident CP-CRE identified from January 2023 through March 2024, medical chart reviews were performed. From 2019-2024, the estimated national pediatric CRE and CP-CRE incidence increased 51% (IRR:1.51; 95% CI:1.22, 1.88) and 92% (IRR:1.92; 95% CI:1.25, 2.99), respectively; increases were similar in the open cohort. Infants had the highest incidence rates. Overall, NDM-CRE incidence increased (IRR: 4.24; 95% CI: 2.07, 9.16), surpassing KPC-CRE as the most prominent carbapenemase. Chart reviews were completed for 109 of 129 pediatric patients with CP-CRE; 14% were in patients without healthcare risk factors. Among patients with healthcare risk factors, 75% had an underlying medical condition; the most common underlying condition among infants and toddlers was cardiovascular disease (64%) and among older children was neurocognitive conditions (49%) and malignancies (41%). Common exposures across all age groups included intensive care unit hospitalization (40%) and healthcare outside the United States (37%). Pediatric CP-CRE incidence is increasing, driven by NDM-CRE for which there are few treatment options. Most cases occurred among children with serious underlying conditions receiving high-acuity care. Prevention opportunities may include admission screening for patients with prior healthcare exposure outside the United States and strengthening infection prevention practices.

title: Essential oils for acute cystitis: a real-world experience in primary care settings
abstract: Acute cystitis is a significant public health challenge, with escalating antimicrobial: resistance threatening conventional antibiotic therapy. Essential oils (EOs) containing bioactive compounds such as carvacrol and cinnamaldehyde, offer multi-target antimicrobial mechanisms that may provide effective alternatives while supporting antimicrobial stewardship efforts. This real-world observational study compared the clinical efficacy of an EO-based formulation with that of standard antibiotic therapy in women with acute cystitis. 68 patients participated: Groups A (N.=24), treated with fosfomycin trometamol 3 g single-dose; Group B (N.=21) received the EO combination (OLEOBIOTICSalud urinaria manufactured by Pranarom International S.A.) at the standard dose (1 capsule 3 times daily for 5 days); Group C (N.=23) received the double dosage. OLEOBIOTICSalud urinaria is a food supplement manufactured by Pranarom International S.A. and formulated with EOs of oregano (Origanum vulgare) 10 mg, Chinese cinnamon (Cinnamomum cassia) 30 mg, lemon (Citrus limon) 5 mg, lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus) 40 mg, thyme (Thymus vulgaris, thymol chemotype) 20 mg, savory (Satureja montana) 20 mg, cloves (Caryophyllus aromaticus) 10 mg, and fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) 15 mg. Primary outcomes was urinary dipstick test negativization. Secondary outcomes assessed symptom severity, patient satisfaction, antibiotic avoidance, and safety profile. Urinary dipstick negativization rates were comparable across groups: Group A 83.3%, Group B 90.5%, and Group C 78.3% (P>0.05). All groups showed a significant improvement in urinary frequency (P<0.001), with patients urinating ≤4 times daily increasing from baseline to post-treatment: Group A from 25.0% to 70.8%, Group B from 19.0% to 85.7%, and Group C from 21.7% to 69.6%. Antibiotic prescription was avoided in 66.7-78.3% of cases. Patient satisfaction was high across all groups, with 71.4% to 100% willing to use the treatment again. Only one adverse event (self-limiting diarrhea) was reported, with no recurrences during follow-up. EO-based formulations demonstrated clinically significant efficacy in the managing of acute cystitis, with high dipstick negativization rates, substantial symptom relief, and excellent safety profile. The multi-target antimicrobial mechanisms of key components offer theoretical advantages for reducing the development of resistance. These findings may support integrating natural treatments into clinical algorithms for uncomplicated cystitis as part of comprehensive antimicrobial stewardship strategies. Nevertheless, randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these real-world observations.

title: Estimating Marginal Effects on Survival Outcomes for Clinical Interpretations and Decision Making
abstract: The Cox regression model is the most widely used method in survival analysis, but the hazard ratio has limited clinical interpretability. Survival or cumulative incidence curves are often used to illustrate treatment effects, yet there is no consensus on the most appropriate methods for generating these curves, particularly in the presence of confounding and competing risks. We reviewed original research articles published in a general medical journal in 2025, identified limitations in common practices, and describe a marginal effects framework to generate adjusted cumulative incidence curves that are coherent with the analysis model, anchored in absolute risk estimates, and adaptable to competing risks and clustered data. The framework targets the population-average difference in cumulative incidence between exposure groups, under the assumptions of no unmeasured confounding, positivity, and non-informative censoring. As a demonstration, we applied the framework to real-world data from Yek et al. (2025) and showed that it produced clinically interpretable estimates of hospital-acquired antimicrobial resistance risk that a single hazard ratio could not convey. To facilitate implementation, we describe each analytic step in detail, discuss available software, and share an R program with core routines written in C for computational efficiency.

title: Porcine Oral Fluid as a Diagnostic Matrix for Tulathromycin and Enrofloxacin Residue Surveillance
abstract: Antibiotic analysis is an important aspect of pig farming due to residues in tissues and the spread of antimicrobial resistance. In vivo control of antimicrobials is particularly significant, especially for the most critical and widely administered drugs. Thus, the aim of this study was to investigate the concentrations of tulathromycin and enrofloxacin in oral fluid after pig treatment. The analysis was performed by an ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS) method. Both drugs were detected for 31 days after the end of the treatment. On the last day of sampling, the concentration of tulathromycin was 19.7 μg/L and that of enrofloxacin was 26.4 μg/L. Tulathromycin reached its peak concentration (2180 μg/L) on day 2, while the highest concentration of enrofloxacin (1250 μg/L) was recorded on day 1 postadministration. The obtained results confirm the feasibility of detecting the two tested compounds in oral fluid, demonstrating a new approach for antemortem antibiotic control in pigs.

title: Antibiotic class shapes O-antigen-dependent phage outcomes in a clinical Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate
abstract: is a high-priority opportunistic pathogen characterized by significant genetic plasticity and increasing multidrug resistance. Although phage-antibiotic combinations are increasingly explored to combat antimicrobial resistance, whether these interactions are synergistic or antagonistic and how different antibiotic classes influence phage replication and the subsequent development of resistance remain unclear. In this study, we examined combinations of the O-antigen-dependent phage phipa10 with amikacin (AMK), levofloxacin (LEV), or meropenem (MEM) againstZS-PA-35. At 24 h, the combinations showed antibiotic-dependent patterns of bacterial growth suppression. High concentrations of amikacin and meropenem reduced the extracellular yield of infectious phipa10. The highest tested levofloxacin concentration also reduced the recovered phage yield. Whole-genome sequencing of phage-resistant mutants showed that meropenem treatment drove large chromosomal deletions encompassingand, resulting in a characteristic brown pigmentation phenotype. LEV-selected isolates carried smaller deletions involving, whereas AMK-selected isolates shared asubstitution. In ainfection model, phipa10-antibiotic combinations improved host survival relative to either treatment alone, although the magnitude of the benefit varied across antibiotic classes. The meropenem combination yielded the highest observed survival proportion despite reduced phage yield. These results show that bacterial suppression, infectious phage yield, and resistance outcomes can diverge among the three tested antibiotic partners.IMPORTANCEPhage-antibiotic combinations may affect bacterial suppression, phage yield, and resistance-associated phenotypes differently. We compared three antibiotic partners in a single-phage system. The observed growth, genetic, and larval survival outcomes varied across the tested treatments. Reduced phage yield did not preclude improved survival in the infection model. These observations support evaluating multiple outcomes when assessing a phage-antibiotic combination. Their broader relevance requires validation with additional isolates, phages, and antibiotics.

title: Stability of therapeutic bacteriophages in clinically approved crystalloid infusion solutions
abstract: The growing burden of antimicrobial resistance underscores the need for effective alternatives to conventional antibiotics, with bacteriophage therapy representing a promising approach. However, insufficient product stability during storage and administration may reduce the delivered dose and confound assessments of clinical efficacy. Clinically approved crystalloid infusion solutions could facilitate phage preparation and administration, but their suitability for phage storage remains poorly characterized. The stability of four virulent bacteriophages targetingorwas evaluated in sodium chloride 0.45%, sodium chloride 0.9%, Ringer's lactate, Ringer's acetate, and saline magnesium (SM) buffer. Phage preparations containing 10⁹ plaque-forming units per mL were stored at 4°C, -20°C, or -80°C, with or without 10% glycerol, for up to 6 months. Phage infectivity was highly dependent on the phage, solution, and storage temperature. Buffered solutions generally preserved infectivity better than saline, particularly under frozen conditions. Glycerol improved stability during freezing, although the magnitude of this effect varied among phages and was most apparent in saline solutions. Storage at -80°C with glycerol provided the most consistent preservation across all four phages, with titers remaining close to baseline. Ringer's solutions supported high stability at -80°C also without glycerol. By contrast, storage at 4°C resulted in greater variability and reduced stability for several phages. These findings demonstrate that clinically approved crystalloid solutions can serve as vehicles for both phage storage and administration and suggest a need for phage-specific stability testing. Reliable bacteriophage therapy requires formulations that preserve phage activity during storage and clinical administration. Yet, standardized approaches to phage formulation and storage remain lacking, and many clinical applications still rely on empirical practices rather than evidence-based pharmaceutical principles. This study addresses an important translational barrier by examining the stability of therapeutically relevant phages targetingandin crystalloid solutions routinely used for intravenous administration. Comparison of distinct phages across different formulations, temperatures, and storage durations demonstrates that stability depends strongly on the individual phage and storage conditions. These findings expand the limited evidence on phage stability in clinically applicable formulations and reinforce the rationale for individual phage stability testing during product development to ensure the delivery of an active and consistent therapeutic dose.
