title: Editorial: Bacteriophages and CRISPR-Cas for combating multidrug-resistant bacteria
Culture-free Helicobacter pylori genomics reveals within-host virulence heterogeneity and antibiotic resistance
abstract: Helicobacter pylori (Hp) infects over 40% of the world population and causes most cases of gastric cancer worldwide, yet fundamental questions about its within-host genetic diversity remain unresolved. Decades of work on Hp genomics depends on culturing clinical isolates, which can distort within-host genetic heterogeneity that informs Hp virulence and antimicrobial resistance. Culture-free alternatives have been limited by the extremely low Hp abundance in gastric tissue (usually 10^-3 to 10^-7 of total genomic DNA), making direct metagenomics prohibitively expensive and existing enrichment strategies insufficient for whole-genome recovery. Here we develop ultra-sensitive Hp sequencing (uHp-seq) for reconstructing Hp genomes directly from gastric biopsies. uHp-seq achieves a thousand-fold Hp DNA enrichment and recovers near-complete genomes across samples spanning orders of magnitude in Hp abundance. Notably, individual hosts may harbor multiple co-existing Hp strains or cagA EPIYA variants with different oncogenic potential. Resistance-associated variants for six commonly used antibiotics are resolved with greater accuracy than PCR-based and probe-based commercial panels. Applied to minimally invasive gastric string samples, uHp-seq delivers reliable resistance profiles without endoscopy, opening a path to genome-guided Hp eradication.

title: Antimicrobial-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the USA: implications of a national surveillance gap
abstract: Surveillance data for Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the USA are distributed across systems designed for different purposes, potentially limiting standardized national surveillance of high-priority resistant phenotypes. We evaluated whether the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS) can support surveillance of multidrug-resistant (MDR) P. aeruginosa and synthesized available CDC surveillance data to characterize the residual surveillance gap. We reviewed the 2026 NNDSS list of nationally notifiable conditions for P. aeruginosa. Because neither P. aeruginosa infection nor a resistant phenotype was present, NNDSS case counts were unable to be analysed. We therefore conducted a descriptive secondary analysis of CDC National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) reports for 2018-21 and the 2022 NHSN Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Option report. In 2018-21 adult NHSN data, 11.9% of tested P. aeruginosa isolates from device-associated infections were MDR, compared with 3.9% from surgical-site infections. Among central-line-associated bloodstream infection isolates, MDR proportions were highest in long-term acute-care hospitals (LTACHs, 25.3%), followed by hospital intensive-care units (14.2%), hospital wards (11.9%) and oncology units (8.5%). Among catheter-associated urinary tract infection isolates, MDR phenotype was observed in 20.8% of LTACH isolates. In the 2022 AR Option report, carbapenem non-susceptibility exceeded 10% among community-onset isolates and approached 20% among hospital-onset isolates. NNDSS cannot currently quantify the burden of MDR P. aeruginosa, but substantial resistance surveillance is available through NHSN and the CDC AR Laboratory Network. The principal gap is not an absence of surveillance data but fragmentation across systems with different populations, denominators, objectives and reporting mechanisms.

title: Shotgun metagenomic characterization of human adenovirus F40 and a non-cpe Clostridium perfringens strain in pediatric prolonged diarrhea: a genome-resolved case study
abstract: Viral and bacterial pathogens may be concurrently detected in pediatric gastroenteritis, yet such findings are often missed by routine diagnostic methods. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing enables comprehensive detection and genomic characterization of microorganisms present in clinical specimens, including pathogens that may not be recovered by conventional testing. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed on a single pediatric diarrheic stool sample, followed by quality filtering, de novo assembly, taxonomic classification, phylogenetic reconstruction, and integrated virulome-resistome profiling, including plasmid-associated resistance elements. Routine diagnostics identified adenovirus as the sole pathogen. Metagenomic analysis confirmed human adenovirus F40 (HAdV-F40), showing close phylogenetic relatedness to globally distributed HAdV-F40 reference strains and a clear distinction from HAdV-F41. In addition, metagenomics uniquely detected a Clostridium perfringens strain (SAM_A8, ST-5) that was not recovered by culture. The strain lacked the classical enterotoxin gene (cpe) but harbored a conserved histotoxic virulence profile, including cpa, pfoA, colA, hyaluronidases, and sialidases. Plasmid-associated tetracycline resistance genes (tetA(P) and tetB(P)) were also identified. This case study demonstrates the feasibility of shotgun metagenomic sequencing for comprehensive detection and genomic characterization of microorganisms present in pediatric diarrheal stool specimens, including organisms not identified by routine diagnostics. The findings are descriptive and highlight the value of metagenomics as a complementary diagnostic approach. However, no conclusions regarding pathogenic synergy, causality, or the clinical contribution of the co-detected organisms can be drawn from this single case.

title: Viral potential to modulate antibiotic resistance gene succession through host interactions during food waste composting
abstract: Composting can mitigate antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) risks, yet viral contributions to their dynamics remain unclear. Using time-series metagenomics, we investigated viral roles in ARG succession during composting of two food waste types. In both composts, ARGs followed an enrichment-decline-rebound trajectory accompanied by substrate-specific ARG-host turnover. Particularly, the maturation rebound involved the re-enrichment of high-risk ARGs, including tet(L) and lnu(G). Procrustes analysis showed significant associations of viral communities with bacterial and ARG profiles. Meanwhile, virus-host networks were organized predominantly around Firmicutes, with both temperate and lytic viral abundances correlated with ARG-host dynamics during the heating-to-thermophilic transition. Viral auxiliary metabolic genes (AMGs), annotated for central carbon metabolism, nutrient acquisition, and stress responses, may aid environmental adaptation in key ARG hosts, including Bacillus spp. Although mobile genetic elements (MGEs) provided important genetic contexts for ARG mobility, only four putative virus-mediated ARG horizontal transfer records were detected. Structural equation modelling suggested potential viral involvement through host interactions, while highlighting the importance of ARG hosts and MGEs in resistome succession. Further viral perturbation experiments are needed to clarify causal contributions in future. Overall, this study provides new insights into viral roles in resistome succession, informing resistance risk management during composting.
